Space complexity: auxiliary space vs total space, space-time tradeoffs, in-place algorithms. P vs NP: P (polynomial time), NP (nondeterministic polynomial), NP-complete (Cook-Levin theorem, SAT), NP-hard, polynomial-time reductions, why P vs NP matters for cryptography and security. Interactive tools: Big O visualizer (plot and compare growth rates), complexity quiz (guess the Big O from code snippets), recurrence solver. 'Algorithms to Live By' connection: computational kindness — when it's OK to use a 'worse' algorithm because the constant factors matter more than asymptotic behavior.

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Data structures deep-dive
sprints.notes: Core data structures with complexity analysis and implementation. Linear structures: arrays (static vs dynamic, amortized doubling), linked lists (singly, doubly, circular), stacks (LIFO — applications: expression evaluation, backtracking, undo), queues (FIFO, circular queue, deque, priority queue). Trees: binary trees, binary search trees (BST — insert, delete, search, traversals: inorder, preorder, postorder, level-order), balanced BSTs (AVL trees — rotations, balance factor; Red-Black trees — properties, recoloring/rotation), B-trees and B+ trees (database indexing, filesystem), heaps (min-heap, max-heap, heapify, heap sort), tries (prefix trees — autocomplete, spell checking, IP routing tables), segment trees, Fenwick trees (BIT). Hash structures: hash tables (hash functions, collision resolution — chaining, open addressing/linear probing/quadratic probing/double hashing, load factor, rehashing), bloom filters (probabilistic membership — false positives, no false negatives, applications in networking/caching), cuckoo hashing. Advanced: disjoint set / union-find (path compression, union by rank), skip lists, LRU cache implementation. For each structure: when to use it, Big O for operations, real-world applications, implementation in Python and C. Interactive visualizations: animated insert/delete/search operations, complexity comparison dashboard. 'Algorithms to Live By' connection: caching chapter (LRU, eviction policies).

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Sorting and searching algorithms
sprints.notes: Sorting and searching — the classics. Comparison sorts: Bubble Sort O(n^2), Selection Sort O(n^2), Insertion Sort O(n^2) — when small/nearly sorted, Merge Sort O(n log n) — stable/divide-and-conquer, Quick Sort O(n log n) average — partition schemes (Lomuto, Hoare), pivot selection (random, median-of-three), Heap Sort O(n log n) — in-place, Shell Sort, Tim Sort (Python/Java default — hybrid merge+insertion). Non-comparison sorts: Counting Sort O(n+k), Radix Sort O(d*(n+k)), Bucket Sort O(n+k). Lower bound proof: comparison sort Omega(n log n) via decision tree model. Searching: linear search O(n), binary search O(log n) — iterative and recursive, interpolation search, exponential search, ternary search. Advanced: external sorting (for data that doesn't fit in memory), parallel sorting algorithms, sorting networks (Batcher's odd-even, bitonic sort). Stability matters: why stable sorts are important for multi-key sorting. For each algorithm: step-by-step trace, complexity analysis (best/worst/average), when to use, implementation in code. Interactive: sorting algorithm visualizer with speed controls, side-by-side race, sorting sound (auditory learning). 'Algorithms to Live By' connection: sorting chapter — the cost of ordering, when to stop sorting and start satisficing.

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Greedy algorithms and dynamic programming
sprints.notes: Two foundational algorithm design paradigms. Greedy algorithms: greedy choice property, optimal substructure, proof of correctness (exchange argument, greedy stays ahead). Classic problems: activity selection (interval scheduling), Huffman coding, fractional knapsack, Dijkstra's (greedy on shortest path), Kruskal's/Prim's (greedy on MST), job scheduling with deadlines, coin change (when greedy works vs when it doesn't). When greedy fails: 0/1 knapsack, TSP, graph coloring — transition to DP. Dynamic programming: overlapping subproblems, optimal substructure, memoization (top-down) vs tabulation (bottom-up), state definition, recurrence formulation. Classic DP problems: Fibonacci (the gateway), 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence (LCS), longest increasing subsequence (LIS), edit distance (Levenshtein — spell checkers, DNA alignment), coin change (minimum coins), matrix chain multiplication, rod cutting, subset sum, partition equal subset. Advanced DP: DP on trees, DP on graphs (shortest paths as DP), bitmask DP (TSP exact solution via Held-Karp O(2^n * n^2)), DP optimization (Knuth's, divide-and-conquer optimization). Security applications: DP in string matching (intrusion detection signatures), optimal resource allocation in incident response. 'Algorithms to Live By' connection: optimal stopping (the 37% rule / secretary problem), explore vs exploit tradeoff.

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Divide and conquer, backtracking, and recursion
sprints.notes: Algorithm design paradigms continued. Recursion mastery: recursive thinking, base cases, recursive leap of faith, call stack visualization, tail recursion, converting recursion to iteration, recursive vs iterative tradeoffs. Divide and conquer: split → solve → combine, Master theorem for analysis. Classic D&C: merge sort, quick sort, binary search, Strassen's matrix multiplication O(n^2.807), closest pair of points O(n log n), Karatsuba multiplication, median of medians (O(n) selection). Backtracking: state-space tree, pruning, constraint satisfaction. Classic problems: N-Queens, Sudoku solver, subset generation, permutation generation, graph coloring, Hamiltonian path, maze solving, word search. Branch and bound: backtracking + bounding function for optimization, 0/1 knapsack via B&B, TSP via B&B (tighter than brute force). Randomized algorithms: Las Vegas vs Monte Carlo, randomized quicksort, randomized primality testing (Miller-Rabin), skip lists, reservoir sampling, random walks. Interactive: recursion call tree visualizer, N-Queens step-through, backtracking maze solver animation. 'Algorithms to Live By' connection: when to explore (backtrack) vs exploit (commit to a path).

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — String algorithms and pattern matching
sprints.notes: String algorithms — critical for security applications. Pattern matching: naive O(n*m), Rabin-Karp (rolling hash), KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt — failure function), Boyer-Moore (bad character + good suffix rules), Aho-Corasick (multi-pattern matching — used in IDS/IPS signature engines like Snort/Suricata). String data structures: suffix arrays, suffix trees (Ukkonen's algorithm), trie-based structures. Advanced: Z-algorithm, longest palindromic substring (Manacher's), regular expression engines (NFA vs DFA construction, Thompson's construction, backtracking regex engines and ReDoS — Regular Expression Denial of Service), approximate string matching (edit distance, fuzzy matching, phonetic algorithms — Soundex, Metaphone). Compression: run-length encoding, Huffman coding (revisited from greedy), LZ77/LZ78, LZW, Burrows-Wheeler Transform (BWT — used in bzip2), dictionary-based compression. Security applications: signature-based intrusion detection (Aho-Corasick in Snort), fuzzy hashing (ssdeep — context-triggered piecewise hashing for malware similarity), ReDoS vulnerability detection and prevention, data loss prevention (DLP) pattern engines. 'Algorithms to Live By' connection: information theory and compression — communicating efficiently.

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Applied algorithms: Algorithms to Live By modules
sprints.notes: Course track inspired by 'Algorithms to Live By' by Brian Christian & Tom Griffiths — mapping each chapter to CS concepts with hands-on applications. Modules: (1) Optimal Stopping — secretary problem, 37% rule, when to stop searching (apartment hunting, hiring, dating), explore/exploit tradeoff. (2) Explore vs Exploit — multi-armed bandit problem, epsilon-greedy, UCB1, Thompson sampling, A/B testing. (3) Sorting — cost of ordering, when NOT to sort, bucket sort for life, search vs sort tradeoffs. (4) Caching — memory hierarchy, LRU eviction, forgetting as feature not bug, cache replacement policies in OS and web. (5) Scheduling — priority queues, shortest job first, weighted completion time, context switching cost, interrupt coalescing. (6) Bayes' Rule — prior/posterior/likelihood, updating beliefs with evidence, Bayesian spam filtering, medical diagnosis. (7) Overfitting — bias-variance tradeoff, cross-validation, regularization, Occam's razor, when simple models beat complex ones. (8) Relaxation — constraint relaxation, Lagrangian relaxation, approximation algorithms, solving hard problems by solving easier ones. (9) Randomness — when randomization beats optimization, simulated annealing, Monte Carlo methods, random sampling. (10) Networking — TCP congestion control as algorithm, exponential backoff, game theory in protocol design. (11) Game Theory — Nash equilibrium, mechanism design, auction theory, price of anarchy. Each module: real-world story → CS theory → interactive simulation → coding exercise → reflection.

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Computational geometry and spatial algorithms
sprints.notes: Computational geometry — algorithms for spatial problems. Fundamentals: point representation, line intersection, cross product for orientation, collinearity. Convex hull: Graham scan O(n log n), Jarvis march O(nh), gift wrapping, divide-and-conquer hull. Closest pair of points: divide-and-conquer O(n log n). Line sweep algorithms: segment intersection (Bentley-Ottmann), closest pair sweep, Voronoi diagrams, Fortune's algorithm. Spatial data structures: k-d trees (nearest neighbor search, range queries), R-trees (spatial indexing for databases), quadtrees/octrees. Range searching: 1D range trees, 2D range trees, fractional cascading. Applications: GIS (geographic information systems), collision detection (games/simulations), motion planning (robotics), geographic routing, geofencing (security — is this device inside the allowed zone?), spatial anomaly detection (unusual login locations). Interactive: convex hull visualizer, k-d tree nearest neighbor animation, Voronoi diagram generator. 'Algorithms to Live By' connection: space-partitioning for efficient search.

sprints.title: The Algorithm Chamber — Algorithm challenges and competition prep
sprints.notes: Competitive programming and algorithm challenge platform. Challenge tiers: Bronze (basic DS + brute force), Silver (sorting + binary search + greedy + simple DP), Gold (graphs + advanced DP + segment trees), Platinum (advanced graph theory + computational geometry + string algorithms + math). Problem sets organized by technique: implement each algorithm from the course on progressively harder problems. Weekly challenges: new problem released each week with editorial solution after deadline. Contest mode: timed problem sets simulating competitive programming contests (Codeforces, LeetCode contest, USACO style). Leaderboard: points by problem difficulty, streak tracking, speed bonuses. Interview prep track: top 100 problems organized by pattern (sliding window, two pointers, BFS/DFS, binary search, DP patterns — knapsack, LCS, intervals), with company tags (FAANG-style questions). Integration with Prime's existing challenge infrastructure (hive engine). Security-themed problems: cryptographic algorithm implementation, network routing optimization, anomaly detection in log data, brute-force complexity estimation for password cracking. 'Algorithms to Live By' bonus round: real-world optimization puzzles from the book.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Design AI/ML hub page and curriculum map
sprints.notes: Design 'The Cortex' — the AI & Machine Learning hub within House of Code. This is a combined AI + ML curriculum that teaches both the theory and hands-on implementation, with a strong cybersecurity application lens throughout. Hub page features: curriculum map showing 4 tracks — (1) AI Foundations & History, (2) Classical Machine Learning, (3) Deep Learning & Neural Networks, (4) AI for Cybersecurity. Difficulty progression: Novice (concepts, no-code tools) → Practitioner (Python + scikit-learn) → Engineer (TensorFlow/PyTorch) → Researcher (custom architectures, papers). Prerequisites: Python fundamentals (cross-reference PL-2), basic statistics/probability (cross-reference CS-2). Hero section with 'AI Timeline' interactive showing key milestones (Turing, perceptron, backprop, ImageNet, AlphaGo, GPT, diffusion models). Quick-start path for students who just want to apply ML to security vs full deep-dive. Register in content-registry.js under code house with 'ai', 'machine-learning', 'deep-learning' topics. Cross-house links to eye (detection), dark-arts (adversarial), shield (defensive AI), script (automation).

sprints.title: The Cortex — AI foundations, history, and ethical frameworks
sprints.notes: AI foundations and context. History: Turing Test (1950), Dartmouth Conference (1956), expert systems era (1970s-80s), AI winters, statistical ML renaissance (1990s-2000s), deep learning revolution (2012 ImageNet — AlexNet), transformer architecture (2017 'Attention Is All You Need'), GPT/BERT/LLM era, generative AI explosion (2022+). Core concepts: what IS intelligence (narrow vs general vs super AI), symbolic AI vs connectionist AI, knowledge representation, search algorithms (BFS, DFS, A*, minimax, alpha-beta pruning), constraint satisfaction, planning. AI categories: supervised vs unsupervised vs reinforcement learning, generative vs discriminative models, parametric vs non-parametric. Ethics and governance: bias in AI (training data bias, algorithmic bias, representation bias), fairness metrics, explainability (XAI — LIME, SHAP), AI regulation (EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF), responsible AI development, deepfake ethics, autonomous weapons debate, job displacement concerns. AI in cybersecurity landscape: where AI is used today (EDR, SIEM, email security, fraud detection, threat intelligence), hype vs reality, AI washing in security products. Interactive: AI timeline explorer, Turing Test simulation, bias detection exercise.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Mathematics for machine learning
sprints.notes: Essential math for understanding ML — not just using APIs, but knowing what's under the hood. Linear algebra: vectors, matrices, matrix operations (multiplication, transpose, inverse), dot product, eigenvalues/eigenvectors (PCA foundation), singular value decomposition (SVD), vector spaces, linear transformations. Calculus: derivatives (chain rule — critical for backpropagation), partial derivatives, gradients, gradient descent (batch, stochastic, mini-batch), learning rate, local vs global minima, saddle points, convexity. Probability and statistics: Bayes' theorem (revisited for ML context), probability distributions (Gaussian/normal, Bernoulli, multinomial, Poisson), maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), maximum a posteriori (MAP), expectation, variance, covariance, correlation, Central Limit Theorem, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals. Information theory: entropy, cross-entropy (loss function), KL divergence, mutual information. Optimization: convex optimization, Lagrange multipliers, constrained optimization, Newton's method, Adam optimizer intuition. Each topic taught with ML motivation first ('why do I need eigenvalues? → PCA dimensionality reduction'). Interactive: gradient descent visualizer (2D and 3D), matrix multiplication animator, probability distribution playground. Cross-references CS-2 (discrete math) for foundational overlap.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Classical machine learning: supervised learning
sprints.notes: Classical supervised learning algorithms. Regression: linear regression (closed-form solution, gradient descent, regularization — L1 Lasso, L2 Ridge, Elastic Net), polynomial regression, logistic regression (binary classification, sigmoid function, decision boundary, multi-class via one-vs-rest/softmax). Decision trees: ID3, C4.5, CART, information gain, Gini impurity, pruning (pre/post), feature importance. Ensemble methods: bagging (Random Forest — how decorrelated trees improve performance), boosting (AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost), stacking. Support Vector Machines: maximum margin classifier, kernel trick (linear, polynomial, RBF, sigmoid), soft margin (C parameter), SVM for text classification. k-Nearest Neighbors: distance metrics (Euclidean, Manhattan, Minkowski, cosine), k selection, curse of dimensionality. Naive Bayes: Gaussian, Multinomial, Bernoulli — spam filtering as classic application. Model evaluation: train/test split, cross-validation (k-fold, stratified, leave-one-out), metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC, confusion matrix, PR curve), overfitting vs underfitting, bias-variance tradeoff. Feature engineering: scaling (StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler), encoding (one-hot, label, target), feature selection (chi-squared, mutual information, recursive elimination). Tools: scikit-learn throughout. Security applications: malware classification, phishing URL detection, spam filtering, network traffic classification.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Classical machine learning: unsupervised learning
sprints.notes: Unsupervised learning for pattern discovery. Clustering: k-Means (initialization — k-means++, elbow method, silhouette score), hierarchical clustering (agglomerative — single/complete/average linkage, dendrograms), DBSCAN (density-based, epsilon, minPts, handling noise), Gaussian Mixture Models (EM algorithm, soft clustering), Mean Shift, spectral clustering. Dimensionality reduction: PCA (principal component analysis — eigendecomposition, explained variance, scree plot), t-SNE (visualization of high-dimensional data, perplexity parameter), UMAP (faster than t-SNE, preserves global structure), autoencoders (neural network-based reduction). Anomaly detection: statistical methods (z-score, IQR), Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, Local Outlier Factor (LOF), Elliptic Envelope, autoencoder-based anomaly detection (reconstruction error threshold). Association rules: Apriori algorithm, FP-Growth, support/confidence/lift — market basket analysis. Topic modeling: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF). Security applications: network anomaly detection (unusual traffic patterns, port scan detection, DGA domain clustering), user behavior analytics (UEBA — insider threat detection), log clustering for SIEM, malware family clustering, threat intelligence grouping. Interactive: k-Means step-through visualizer, PCA/t-SNE explorer, anomaly detection playground with synthetic data. Cross-references eye house for monitoring/detection applications.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Deep learning fundamentals and neural networks
sprints.notes: Neural networks from perceptron to modern architectures. Foundations: biological inspiration (neuron model), perceptron (single-layer, linear separability, XOR problem), multi-layer perceptron (MLP), activation functions (sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, Leaky ReLU, GELU, Swish — why ReLU solved vanishing gradients). Training: forward propagation, loss functions (MSE, cross-entropy, hinge), backpropagation (chain rule applied, computational graph), gradient descent variants (SGD, momentum, RMSprop, Adam, AdamW), learning rate scheduling (step decay, cosine annealing, warmup), batch normalization, dropout, weight initialization (Xavier, He). Architecture design: fully connected layers, hidden layer sizing, depth vs width tradeoffs, skip connections (ResNet insight), universal approximation theorem. Practical deep learning: data preprocessing (normalization, augmentation), training pipeline (DataLoader, epochs, batching), overfitting mitigation (early stopping, regularization, data augmentation), hyperparameter tuning (grid search, random search, Bayesian optimization — Optuna), transfer learning (fine-tuning pretrained models). Frameworks: PyTorch (primary — tensors, autograd, nn.Module, training loop), TensorFlow/Keras (secondary — Sequential/Functional API, tf.data), comparison and when to use each. Hardware: GPU training (CUDA basics), TPU overview, cloud ML platforms (AWS SageMaker, GCP Vertex AI, Azure ML). Interactive: neural network playground (TensorFlow Playground style but built in Prime), backpropagation step-through visualizer, loss landscape explorer.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Convolutional Neural Networks and computer vision
sprints.notes: CNNs and computer vision. CNN architecture: convolution operation (filters/kernels, stride, padding, feature maps), pooling (max, average, global average), receptive field, parameter sharing. Classic architectures: LeNet (handwriting), AlexNet (ImageNet breakthrough), VGG (depth matters), GoogLeNet/Inception (width + depth), ResNet (skip connections — 152 layers), DenseNet, EfficientNet (compound scaling), MobileNet (lightweight for mobile). Tasks: image classification, object detection (R-CNN family, YOLO — You Only Look Once, SSD), semantic segmentation (U-Net, DeepLab), instance segmentation (Mask R-CNN), image generation (GANs, diffusion models). Transfer learning for vision: ImageNet pretrained models, fine-tuning strategies (freeze layers, discriminative learning rates), domain adaptation. Data augmentation: geometric transforms (flip, rotate, crop, scale), color augmentation, mixup, cutout, AutoAugment. Tools: torchvision, OpenCV, Pillow, albumentations. Security applications: CAPTCHA solving/breaking, deepfake detection (face manipulation artifacts), malware visualization (binary-to-image classification — converting executables to grayscale images), phishing page visual similarity detection, OCR for document analysis in forensics, surveillance system analysis. Interactive: CNN filter visualization (what does each layer learn?), real-time object detection demo, style transfer playground.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Recurrent Neural Networks and sequence modeling
sprints.notes: Sequence modeling — from RNNs to attention. RNN fundamentals: sequential data, hidden state, unrolling through time, vanishing/exploding gradients. LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory): cell state, gates (forget, input, output), why LSTM solves vanishing gradients. GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit): simplified LSTM, reset/update gates, GRU vs LSTM tradeoffs. Bidirectional RNNs: forward + backward context. Sequence-to-sequence: encoder-decoder architecture, teacher forcing, beam search decoding. Attention mechanism: Bahdanau attention (additive), Luong attention (multiplicative), self-attention, the breakthrough insight — 'Attention Is All You Need'. Transformers: multi-head self-attention, positional encoding, encoder-decoder structure, layer normalization, feedforward layers, why transformers replaced RNNs (parallelization, long-range dependencies). Applications: text classification, sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, machine translation, time series forecasting, speech recognition basics. Security applications: log sequence analysis (detecting anomalous command sequences), network traffic time-series anomaly detection, DGA detection (character-level LSTM), malicious PowerShell command detection, predictive threat modeling. Interactive: RNN unrolling animation, attention heatmap visualizer, sequence generation demo (character-level text generation).

sprints.title: The Cortex — Natural Language Processing and LLMs
sprints.notes: NLP from classical to large language models. Classical NLP: tokenization (word, subword — BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece), stemming/lemmatization, stopwords, bag-of-words, TF-IDF, n-grams, word embeddings (Word2Vec — CBOW/Skip-gram, GloVe, FastText). Transformer-based NLP: BERT (bidirectional, masked language model, fine-tuning for downstream tasks), GPT family (autoregressive, next-token prediction, scaling laws), T5 (text-to-text), RoBERTa, DistilBERT, XLNet. Large Language Models: architecture deep-dive (decoder-only, billions of parameters), pretraining (next-token prediction on internet-scale data), instruction tuning, RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback), Constitutional AI, DPO. Using LLMs: API usage (Claude API, OpenAI API), prompt engineering (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, system prompts), RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation — embedding, vector databases, chunking), fine-tuning (LoRA, QLoRA, full fine-tuning), agents and tool use. LLM evaluation: benchmarks (MMLU, HumanEval, GSM8K), hallucination detection, perplexity. Security applications: phishing email detection (NLP classification), threat intelligence report parsing (NER for IoCs), security log summarization, automated vulnerability description analysis, malware report generation. Security OF LLMs: prompt injection (direct, indirect), jailbreaking, data poisoning, training data extraction, model inversion, membership inference. Cross-references dark-arts for offensive AI techniques.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Reinforcement learning
sprints.notes: Reinforcement learning — agents that learn from interaction. Foundations: agent, environment, state, action, reward, policy, value function, Markov Decision Process (MDP), Bellman equation, discount factor (gamma), exploration vs exploitation (epsilon-greedy, UCB, Thompson sampling — connects to CS-10 Algorithms to Live By). Classical RL: Monte Carlo methods, Temporal Difference learning (TD(0), TD(lambda)), Q-learning (off-policy, tabular), SARSA (on-policy). Deep RL: Deep Q-Network (DQN — experience replay, target network, Atari breakthrough), Double DQN, Dueling DQN, Prioritized Experience Replay. Policy gradient methods: REINFORCE, Actor-Critic (A2C, A3C), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO — current workhorse), Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO). Advanced: multi-agent RL (MARL — cooperation, competition), model-based RL (World Models, MuZero), offline RL, reward shaping, sim-to-real transfer, RLHF for LLMs (connecting back to ML-9). Environments: OpenAI Gymnasium (CartPole, LunarLander, Atari), custom environments, PettingZoo (multi-agent). Security applications: adaptive penetration testing agents (automated attack path discovery), dynamic firewall rule optimization, adaptive honeypot behavior, intrusion response automation, adversarial RL for testing security policies, autonomous cyber defense agents. Interactive: GridWorld RL visualizer, Q-table heatmap, policy gradient training demo. Connection to Colosseum game mechanics — RL agent that could play Hexworth Arena card game.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Generative AI (GANs, diffusion models, and beyond)

Variational Autoencoders: encoder-decoder, latent space, KL divergence, reparameterization trick, VAE vs GAN tradeoffs, beta-VAE. Diffusion models: forward process (adding noise), reverse process (denoising), U-Net backbone, noise schedules, classifier-free guidance, DDPM, DDIM. Text-to-image: DALL-E, Stable Diffusion (architecture, latent diffusion, CLIP text encoder), Midjourney, controllable generation (ControlNet, IP-Adapter). Audio generation: text-to-speech (neural TTS), voice cloning, music generation. Video generation: Sora-like architectures (temporal transformers). Security implications: deepfake generation and detection (face swap, lip sync, full body), synthetic voice attacks (vishing with cloned voices), AI-generated phishing content, data augmentation for training security models (generating synthetic malware samples), copyright and IP concerns. Deepfake detection: visual artifacts, temporal inconsistencies, frequency analysis, detection models (FaceForensics++, Microsoft Video Authenticator). Cross-references dark-arts for offensive applications.

sprints.title: The Cortex — Adversarial machine learning and AI security

Data poisoning: backdoor attacks (BadNets, Trojan attacks), clean-label attacks, data poisoning for model degradation, label flipping. Model attacks: model extraction (stealing model parameters via API queries), membership inference (was this data point in training set?), model inversion (reconstructing training data), training data extraction from LLMs. Defenses: adversarial training (augmenting with adversarial examples), certified defenses (randomized smoothing, interval bound propagation), input preprocessing (feature squeezing, JPEG compression), model robustness evaluation (AutoAttack benchmark), differential privacy for training, federated learning security. ML supply chain: model serialization attacks (pickle deserialization in PyTorch — arbitrary code execution), Hugging Face model hub security, poisoned pretrained models, dependency attacks in ML pipelines. MITRE ATLAS: Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems — tactics, techniques, and case studies. Red teaming AI: systematic evaluation methodology, jailbreak taxonomies, automated red teaming. Labs: craft adversarial examples against image classifier, backdoor attack demonstration, model extraction via API queries, LLM jailbreak exercise. Cross-references dark-arts (offensive) and shield (defensive).

sprints.title: The Cortex — ML for cybersecurity: detection and defense

Network security: network intrusion detection with ML (NSL-KDD, CICIDS datasets), flow-based classification, encrypted traffic analysis (without decryption — metadata, timing, size features), DGA domain detection (Random Forest, LSTM), DNS tunneling detection. Malware analysis: static analysis features (PE headers, imported functions, file entropy, string analysis), dynamic analysis features (API call sequences, system call graphs, network behavior), malware family classification, zero-day malware detection via anomaly detection, EMBER dataset. Email security: phishing detection (URL features, email header analysis, NLP on body text, visual similarity of phishing pages), BEC (Business Email Compromise) detection. User behavior analytics: insider threat detection (baseline behavior modeling, anomaly scoring), account compromise detection (impossible travel, unusual access patterns, credential abuse patterns). SOC automation: alert triage ML (priority scoring, false positive reduction), automated incident classification, SOAR integration. Threat intelligence: IoC enrichment with ML, threat actor attribution, dark web monitoring with NLP. Practical pipeline: data collection → feature engineering → model selection → training → evaluation → deployment → monitoring → retraining. MLOps for security: model drift detection, continuous retraining, A/B testing models, explainability for SOC analysts (why did the model alert?). Labs: build a phishing URL detector, train malware classifier on EMBER, anomaly detection on network flow data. Cross-references eye and shield houses.

sprints.title: The Cortex — MLOps, deployment, and production ML

CI/CD for ML: automated testing (data validation, model performance tests, A/B testing), pipeline orchestration (Kubeflow, Airflow, Prefect), feature stores (Feast), monitoring (data drift, concept drift, model degradation). Responsible deployment: model cards, bias auditing before deployment, canary deployments, rollback strategies, incident response for ML systems. Security: model serving attack surface, API authentication, rate limiting, input validation, adversarial input detection in production. Cross-references cloud house for infrastructure.

Filters: minimum 10 stars, has license file, last updated within 2 years, contains markdown/HTML/PDF/PPTX content (not just code tools). Output: per-repo JSON record with metadata, content preview, and Hexworth house recommendation. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js scan --topic cybersecurity --min-stars 10.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — GitLab and alternative platform scrapers
sprints.notes: Extend Repo Scout beyond GitHub to other platforms. GitLab: use GitLab API (v4) to search public projects with cybersecurity/education topics. Many university courses host on GitLab (self-hosted instances and gitlab.com). Bitbucket: search public repos — less common for edu content but some exist. SourceHut: niche but growing, some security research hosted here. Academic sources: (1) MIT OpenCourseWare — scrape course listings for computer science and cybersecurity, find linked GitHub repos or downloadable materials. (2) Coursera/edX — identify open-source companion repos for security courses. (3) Open Textbook Library — search for CC-licensed cybersecurity and networking textbooks. (4) Archive.org — search for archived educational materials with permissive licenses. Non-repo content sources: (5) SlideShare/SpeakerDeck — scrape for cybersecurity presentation decks with CC licenses. (6) NIST/CISA public resources — training materials, frameworks, guides (all public domain). Each platform gets its own scraper module under _tools/repo-scout/scrapers/. Common output format so all discoveries feed into the same manifest.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — Content classifier and house mapper
sprints.notes: Build an automated classifier that analyzes discovered repos and maps them to Hexworth houses. Analysis steps: (1) File type inventory — count markdown, HTML, PPTX, PDF, Jupyter notebooks, YAML, code files to determine content type (lecture slides, labs, reference docs, tools). (2) Keyword extraction — scan README and top-level docs for domain keywords: map to houses using keyword → house lookup table (e.g., 'firewall' → shield/web, 'malware' → dark-arts, 'AWS' → cloud, 'subnet' → web, 'Arduino' → forge, 'Python' → code, 'cryptography' → key, 'SIEM' → eye, 'PowerShell' → script). (3) License classifier — categorize license permissiveness (Public Domain > CC0 > MIT > Apache 2.0 > CC-BY > CC-BY-SA > GPL > CC-BY-NC > proprietary/unknown). Flag non-commercial licenses as 'review required'. (4) Quality scoring — composite score based on: stars, forks, recency, content volume, file organization, README quality, license permissiveness. (5) Conversion effort estimator — small (< 10 files, simple markdown), medium (10-50 files, mixed formats), large (50+ files or complex PPTX/PDF conversion). Output: enriched discovery record with house[], contentType, license, qualityScore, conversionEffort, recommended priority. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js classify --input discoveries.json.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — Discovery dashboard and review workflow
sprints.notes: Build a dashboard to review, approve, and track discovered repos. Features: (1) Discovery browser — filterable/sortable table of all discovered repos: name, URL, house mapping, quality score, license, conversion effort, status (new/reviewed/approved/forked/converting/converted/rejected). (2) Review workflow — click a discovery to see full details: README preview, file tree, content samples, license text, similar repos already in pipeline. Mark as 'approve for fork', 'reject' (with reason), or 'bookmark for later'. (3) Fork tracker — once approved, track the fork process: forked → content extracted → conversion sprint created → conversion in progress → integrated into Prime. (4) Stats dashboard — total discoveries, by house, by license, by status, conversion pipeline metrics. (5) Scheduled scanning — configure cron/scheduled task to run scrapers weekly and surface new discoveries. (6) Duplicate detection — flag repos that contain substantially similar content to already-forked repos or existing Prime content. Build as HTML page in _tools/repo-scout/dashboard.html or as CLI reports: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js dashboard, node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js report --format md.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — Auto-fork and content extraction pipeline
sprints.notes: Automate the fork → extract → stage pipeline. Auto-fork: use GitHub API (or gh CLI) to fork approved repos to the FM-256 GitHub organization. Naming convention: hexworth-source-{original-repo-name}. Content extraction: (1) Clone the forked repo locally to _planning/repo-scout-imports/{repo-name}/. (2) Extract convertible content — PPTX files (use python-pptx to extract text + images), PDF files (extract text with PyMuPDF/pdfplumber), Markdown files (copy directly), Jupyter notebooks (extract cells), HTML slides (copy directly). (3) Generate a conversion manifest: source file → target Prime file mapping, with house assignment and module numbering. (4) Auto-create sprint items — for each repo, generate EHE-style sprint items in sprints.json for the conversion work (one item per module/chapter). Safeguards: never auto-fork without approval flag, never overwrite existing Prime content, always preserve attribution and license in extracted content. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js fork RS-{id}, node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js extract {repo-name}.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — License compliance and attribution tracker
sprints.notes: Build a license compliance system to ensure all forked and converted content respects original licenses. Components: (1) License database — for every forked repo, store: original license text, license type (SPDX identifier), original author(s), original URL, fork date, any license conditions (attribution required, share-alike, non-commercial). (2) Attribution generator — automatically generate attribution notices for converted content. Each Prime module converted from external source gets a footer or metadata field: 'Adapted from [Original Title] by [Author], licensed under [License]. Original: [URL]'. (3) License compatibility matrix — which licenses allow what: can we modify? must we share-alike? can we use commercially? must we attribute? (4) Compliance checker — scan _planning/repo-scout-imports/ and cross-reference with license database, flag any content lacking license info or using incompatible licenses. (5) NOTICE file — maintain a master NOTICE.md listing all third-party content sources, licenses, and attribution. This is non-negotiable — protects Hexworth legally and respects open-source community. Store at _tools/repo-scout/licenses.json and generate NOTICE.md.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — Conversion template engine for common formats
sprints.notes: Build reusable conversion templates to speed up the raw-to-Prime pipeline. Templates needed: (1) PPTX → Presentation HTML — extract slides from PowerPoint, convert to Prime slide-based presentation format with correct house theme (auto-detect house from RS-4 classification). Handle: text extraction, bullet points, images (export to assets/), tables, code blocks, speaker notes. (2) Markdown → Presentation HTML — convert structured markdown (headings = slides) to Prime presentation format. (3) PDF → Presentation HTML — extract pages/sections, OCR if scanned, convert to slides. (4) Jupyter Notebook → Lab HTML — convert notebook cells to Prime interactive lab format. (5) Quiz/Test Bank → Quiz HTML — parse common test bank formats (CSV, QTI, Respondus, plain text Q&A) into Prime quiz format. Each template: auto-applies correct house color palette, adds Hexworth navigation chrome, generates content-registry.js entry stub, creates progress tracking hooks. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/convert.js --input source.pptx --house dark-arts --module-id ehe-01 --type presentation. This is the force multiplier — makes bulk conversion feasible instead of hand-building every module.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — Initial seed scan and first batch fork
sprints.notes: Run the first production scan and fork the initial batch of high-value repos. Target: 50-100 discovered repos, fork top 10-20 highest-quality finds. Priority search targets by house: Dark Arts (ethical hacking courses, CTF writeup collections, pentest methodology repos), Web (networking courses, CCNA/Network+ study materials, protocol labs), Cloud (AWS/Azure/GCP security courses, cloud architecture materials), Code (programming courses with security focus, algorithm visualizations), Shield (GRC frameworks, compliance guides, risk assessment templates), Key (cryptography courses, crypto challenge sets), Eye (SIEM/SOC training materials, log analysis courses, threat hunting playbooks), Script (automation courses, scripting tutorials, DevOps security), Forge (hardware hacking, IoT security, embedded systems courses). Deliverable: first discoveries.json populated, first batch of forks completed, conversion sprints auto-generated for top 5 repos. This proves the pipeline end-to-end and starts feeding fresh content into the conversion queue.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Hardware inventory, drive assessment, and BIOS/UEFI setup
sprints.notes: Physical setup and inventory of the Neon main server. Tasks: (1) Document hardware specs — CPU, RAM (total and configuration), motherboard model, NIC(s), GPU if any, PSU wattage. (2) Inventory all hard drives — make, model, capacity, interface (SATA, NVMe, SAS), current health (SMART data), RPM/type (HDD vs SSD). (3) Decide drive layout strategy: which drive(s) for OS, which for data/databases, which for backups, any hot spares. (4) BIOS/UEFI configuration — boot order, enable virtualization (VT-x/AMD-V, VT-d/IOMMU if needed), AHCI mode for SATA, NVMe configuration, fan/thermal settings, wake-on-LAN if desired. (5) Check/update firmware — BIOS, drive firmware, NIC firmware, RAID controller firmware if applicable. (6) Physical setup — rack/shelf placement, power connections (UPS if available), network cabling (at least 1 Gbps, ideally 2.5/10G if hardware supports), KVM or remote management (IPMI/iLO/iDRAC if server-grade). Deliverable: hardware manifest document and drive layout plan approved before OS install.

sprints.title: Neon Server — OS installation and base system configuration
sprints.notes: Install and configure the base operating system on Neon. Decisions: (1) OS selection — Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS (stable, wide support, 5-year maintenance), Debian 12 (rock-solid, minimal), Rocky Linux 9 / AlmaLinux 9 (RHEL-based, enterprise), or Proxmox VE (if running VMs/containers as primary workload). (2) Disk partitioning — recommended layout: boot partition (1GB, ext4), root partition (50-100GB SSD, ext4/xfs), swap (1-2x RAM or 8GB cap), /home (SSD, user data), /var (separate partition for logs/databases, SSD), /data (large HDD pool for bulk storage — mounted separately). Consider LVM for flexible resizing. (3) RAID configuration — if multiple drives: RAID 1 for OS (mirror for redundancy), RAID 5/6 or ZFS raidz1/raidz2 for data pool (capacity with parity), or ZFS mirror pairs. ZFS preferred if RAM allows (1GB per TB of storage). (4) Base config — hostname (neon), static IP on LAN, SSH server (key-only auth, disable password auth, non-standard port optional), firewall (ufw or firewalld — deny all, allow SSH), timezone, NTP sync, automatic security updates (unattended-upgrades). (5) User setup — admin user, sudo group, SSH key deployment from dev machines.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Storage pool setup and mount strategy
sprints.notes: Configure storage pools and mount points for organized data management. Tasks: (1) Create storage pools — if using ZFS: create zpools (tank, fast-pool for SSDs, bulk-pool for HDDs), set compression (lz4), set atime=off, create datasets for each purpose. If using LVM: create volume groups and logical volumes. If using mdadm RAID: create arrays, format, mount. (2) Mount point structure: /data/hexworth/ (Hexworth project repos and working copies), /data/databases/ (database data directories), /data/backups/ (automated backup target), /data/media/ (raw source content — PPTX, PDF, videos), /data/repos/ (forked GitHub repos from Repo Scout), /data/scratch/ (temp workspace for conversions). (3) Permissions — create hexworth group, set proper ownership and permissions on each mount point, ACLs if needed for multi-user access. (4) fstab entries — ensure all mounts persist across reboots with correct options (noatime, nofail for non-critical). (5) Monitoring — set up disk space alerts (df thresholds), SMART monitoring (smartmontools + smartd for drive health alerts), ZFS scrub schedule if using ZFS (monthly). (6) Network shares — Samba share for Windows access from dev machines, NFS for Linux clients, or both. Ensure Hexworth project data is accessible from the WSL development environment.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Database server installation (PostgreSQL + MongoDB)
sprints.notes: Install and configure database servers on Neon. PostgreSQL (relational): (1) Install PostgreSQL 16 (latest stable). (2) Configure postgresql.conf — listen_addresses (LAN IP or 0.0.0.0), port 5432, shared_buffers (25% of RAM), effective_cache_size (75% of RAM), work_mem, maintenance_work_mem, WAL settings for durability. (3) Configure pg_hba.conf — local auth (peer/md5), LAN access (md5/scram-sha-256, restrict to subnet). (4) Create databases: hexworth_prime (Prime platform data), hexworth_arena (Arena game data), hexworth_colosseum (Colosseum game data), hexworth_analytics (usage analytics, progress tracking). (5) Create application user(s) with least-privilege roles. MongoDB (document store): (1) Install MongoDB 7.x Community. (2) Configure mongod.conf — bindIp (LAN), port 27017, storage.dbPath (/data/databases/mongodb), enable authentication. (3) Create databases: hexworth_content (content registry, course materials), hexworth_users (user profiles, progress). (4) Create application users with appropriate roles. Both: (5) Firewall rules — allow DB ports only from trusted LAN IPs. (6) Verify connectivity from dev machines. (7) Basic backup scripts (pg_dump, mongodump) running on cron to /data/backups/.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Network configuration and remote access
sprints.notes: Configure Neon's network for reliable LAN access and optional remote access. LAN setup: (1) Static IP assignment — either static in netplan/NetworkManager or DHCP reservation on router. (2) Hostname resolution — add neon to /etc/hosts on dev machines, or set up local DNS (Pi-hole, dnsmasq) so 'neon' or 'neon.local' resolves from all devices. (3) mDNS/Avahi — install avahi-daemon so neon.local works via mDNS (zero-config). (4) Firewall rules — allow: SSH (22 or custom), PostgreSQL (5432), MongoDB (27017), Samba (445), NFS (2049), HTTP/HTTPS (80/443 for future web services), monitoring (9090 Prometheus, 3000 Grafana). Deny all else. Remote access (optional): (5) Tailscale or WireGuard VPN — secure tunnel for accessing Neon from outside LAN without exposing ports to internet. Tailscale is zero-config; WireGuard is lighter but manual. (6) SSH jump host — if no VPN, SSH on non-standard port with fail2ban for brute-force protection. (7) Dynamic DNS — if ISP gives dynamic IP, set up DDNS (DuckDNS, Cloudflare, No-IP) for consistent remote hostname. (8) Speed test — verify network throughput between dev machines and Neon (iperf3).

sprints.title: Neon Server — Docker and container runtime setup
sprints.notes: Install Docker and container infrastructure on Neon for running services. Tasks: (1) Install Docker Engine (not Docker Desktop — server has no GUI). Add docker group, add admin user to docker group. (2) Install Docker Compose v2 (plugin). (3) Configure Docker — data-root on data drive (not OS drive), default logging driver (json-file with max-size/max-file rotation), DNS settings, default network. (4) Set up docker-compose project structure: /data/hexworth/docker/ with per-service compose files. (5) Initial containers to consider: Portainer (web UI for managing containers), Nginx Proxy Manager or Traefik (reverse proxy for web services), Watchtower (auto-update containers), Uptime Kuma (service monitoring). (6) Container networking — create hexworth-net bridge network for inter-container communication. (7) Volume strategy — named volumes stored on data drives, bind mounts for config files. (8) If databases end up containerized instead of bare-metal (NE-4), set up persistent volumes on data drives with proper backup hooks. Docker gives flexibility to spin up dev/staging environments, run Repo Scout scrapers in containers, or add services like Redis, Elasticsearch, or MinIO later without cluttering the base OS.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Backup strategy and disaster recovery
sprints.notes: Set up automated backups and a disaster recovery plan. Backup targets: (1) Databases — pg_dump (PostgreSQL) and mongodump (MongoDB) nightly to /data/backups/db/ with 7-day rotation. (2) Configuration — /etc/ configs, Docker compose files, cron jobs, firewall rules — backed up weekly. (3) Hexworth project data — git repos are self-backed-up to GitHub, but local working copies and non-git data (raw source content, converted assets, uploaded media) need backup. (4) Backup destination — local backup drive (separate physical drive from data drives), plus off-site: rsync to a cloud storage bucket (Backblaze B2 is cheapest at $5/TB/month), or rsync to a second machine. Tools: (5) restic or borg for deduplicated, encrypted, incremental backups. (6) Cron schedule: databases nightly, full system weekly, configs on change. (7) Backup verification — monthly test restore to confirm backups are valid (untested backups are not backups). (8) Disaster recovery runbook — document: how to rebuild Neon from scratch, where backups live, restore order (OS → storage → databases → services → data), estimated recovery time. Store runbook in the repo, not only on Neon.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Monitoring, alerting, and health dashboard
sprints.notes: Set up monitoring so you know when something goes wrong before it becomes a problem. Stack: (1) Prometheus (metrics collection) — node_exporter for system metrics (CPU, RAM, disk, network, temperature), postgres_exporter for PostgreSQL metrics, mongodb_exporter for MongoDB metrics. (2) Grafana (dashboards) — system overview dashboard (CPU, RAM, disk I/O, network throughput, temperatures), database dashboard (connections, query performance, cache hit ratio, replication lag), Docker dashboard (container status, resource usage), storage dashboard (pool usage, SMART health, ZFS scrub status). (3) Alerting — Grafana alerts or Alertmanager: disk space > 85%, CPU sustained > 90%, RAM > 90%, drive SMART warning, database connection failures, backup job failures, container crash/restart. Notification channels: email, Slack/Discord webhook, or Pushover for mobile push. (4) Uptime Kuma — simple uptime monitor for all services (HTTP endpoints, TCP ports, Docker containers), public status page optional. (5) Log aggregation (optional) — Loki + Promtail for centralized log searching, or simple logrotate + journald for basics. All monitoring services run as Docker containers (NE-6).

sprints.title: Neon Server — Security hardening and access control
sprints.notes: Harden Neon against attack — practice what Hexworth teaches. SSH hardening: (1) Key-only authentication (disable PasswordAuthentication), (2) disable root login, (3) AllowUsers whitelist, (4) fail2ban for brute-force protection (ban after 5 failed attempts, 1-hour ban). Firewall: (5) ufw/firewalld — default deny incoming, explicit allow per service, rate-limit SSH. System hardening: (6) Automatic security updates (unattended-upgrades on Ubuntu/Debian, dnf-automatic on RHEL-based). (7) Remove unnecessary services (telnet, FTP, avahi if not needed). (8) Disable unused network protocols (IPv6 if not used). (9) File integrity monitoring — AIDE or Tripwire for detecting unauthorized changes to system files. (10) AppArmor or SELinux — enforce mandatory access controls. (11) Kernel hardening — sysctl settings (disable IP forwarding unless routing, enable SYN cookies, disable ICMP redirects). (12) User audit — review /etc/passwd, no shared accounts, strong passwords for any non-key accounts. (13) Regular vulnerability scanning — run Lynis audit monthly, review findings. (14) Logging — ensure auditd is running for security event logging, forward logs to centralized location. This is Hexworth's own server — it should be a model of the security practices we teach.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Dev environment integration and workflow connection
sprints.notes: Connect Neon to the daily development workflow so it's actually used, not forgotten. Dev machine integration: (1) Mount Neon shares on WSL — Samba mount in /etc/fstab or systemd automount so /mnt/neon/hexworth is always available. (2) Database connection profiles — set up .pgpass and mongosh connection strings on dev machines for quick DB access. (3) VS Code Remote-SSH — configure VS Code to connect to Neon for editing files directly on server when needed. (4) Git workflow — option A: continue developing locally, push to GitHub, Neon pulls from GitHub (webhook or cron). Option B: develop on Neon via SSH/Remote, push to GitHub from Neon. Option C: local dev + Neon as CI/staging (git push triggers Neon deploy). (5) Repo Scout integration — configure _tools/repo-scout to write discoveries to Neon's database instead of local JSON. (6) Content pipeline — raw source content (PPTX, PDF from EHE, forked repos) stored on Neon's bulk storage, accessed from dev machines via network share. (7) Firebase sync — option to run Firebase CLI from Neon for deployments (firebase deploy from server). (8) Alias/shortcut setup — add ssh aliases and shell functions to .bashrc on dev machines for quick Neon access (ssh neon, neon-db, neon-logs).

sprints.title: API Foundations — REST Architecture, HTTP Methods & Status Codes
sprints.notes: Module 1: What is an API, REST vs SOAP vs GraphQL, HTTP methods (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE), status codes (2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx), request/response anatomy (headers, body, query params). Interactive lab: explore a live API using built-in HTTP client simulator. Quiz on methods and status codes.

sprints.title: API Foundations — Authentication & Authorization (API Keys, OAuth, JWT)
sprints.notes: Module 2: API keys, Bearer tokens, OAuth 2.0 flows (authorization code, client credentials), JWT structure (header.payload.signature), token expiration and refresh. Interactive lab: decode a JWT, identify claims, spot an expired token. Lab 2: walk through an OAuth flow step-by-step. Quiz on auth patterns.

sprints.title: API Foundations — API Design & Documentation (OpenAPI/Swagger)
sprints.notes: Module 3: RESTful naming conventions, resource modeling, versioning strategies (URI vs header), pagination, filtering, sorting. OpenAPI/Swagger spec walkthrough — read and interpret a spec file. Interactive lab: given a business requirement, design API endpoints. Lab 2: read a Swagger doc and answer questions about available endpoints.

sprints.title: API Foundations — Rate Limiting, Throttling & Error Handling
sprints.notes: Module 4: Rate limiting (token bucket, sliding window), 429 Too Many Requests, retry-after headers, exponential backoff. Error response patterns (RFC 7807 problem details). Idempotency keys. Interactive lab: simulate hitting a rate limit, implement backoff logic. Quiz on error handling best practices.

sprints.title: API Security — OWASP API Top 10
sprints.notes: Module 5: OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023): BOLA, broken authentication, broken object property level authorization, unrestricted resource consumption, broken function level authorization, server-side request forgery, security misconfiguration, lack of protection from automated threats, improper asset management, unsafe consumption of APIs. Real-world breach examples for each. Interactive lab: identify vulnerabilities in sample API code snippets. Quiz.

sprints.title: API Security — Hands-On API Penetration Testing
sprints.notes: Module 6: API recon (endpoint discovery, parameter fuzzing), testing for BOLA (IDOR), broken auth bypass, mass assignment, injection via API params, SSRF via webhook URLs. Tools: Burp Suite, Postman, curl, ffuf for API fuzzing. Interactive CTF-style lab: exploit a vulnerable API (3-4 flags to capture). Builds on Ancient Ledger pattern but API-focused.

sprints.title: Cloud APIs — AWS, Azure & GCP API Patterns
sprints.notes: Module 7: Cloud provider APIs — AWS (IAM SigV4 signing, SDK patterns, API Gateway, Lambda integration), Azure (Azure AD tokens, Management API, Azure Functions HTTP triggers), GCP (service account auth, Cloud Endpoints, Cloud Functions). Comparing approaches across providers. Interactive lab: make authenticated calls to simulated cloud APIs. Quiz on cloud API patterns.

sprints.title: API Foundations — Webhooks, WebSockets & Event-Driven APIs
sprints.notes: Module 8: Beyond REST — webhooks (push vs pull, signature verification, retry logic), WebSockets (persistent connections, real-time data), Server-Sent Events, gRPC basics. When to use which pattern. Interactive lab: set up a webhook receiver, verify payload signatures. Lab 2: WebSocket chat simulator. Quiz.

sprints.title: API Capstone — Build & Secure a Full API
sprints.notes: Capstone project: students design, build, and secure a complete API in a guided simulator. Requirements: proper resource modeling, authentication (JWT), input validation, rate limiting, error handling, CORS configuration, logging. Then pen-test their own API for OWASP Top 10 issues. Graded on both functionality and security posture. Completion unlocks API Architect achievement.

sprints.title: Code Armory — Python Graphics (turtle, pygame, matplotlib, tkinter)
sprints.notes: Python graphics curriculum. Fundamentals: turtle module (drawing, loops, patterns, fractals), tkinter GUI basics (windows, widgets, event handling, canvas drawing). Intermediate: matplotlib (plots, charts, subplots, styling, animation), Pillow/PIL (image manipulation, filters, compositing). Advanced: pygame (game loops, sprites, collision detection, sound, simple 2D games), procedural art generation, data visualization dashboards. Projects: fractal generator, snake game, data dashboard, image filter tool, interactive drawing app.

sprints.title: Code Armory — Add neon purple accents to Zero to Python hub

Targets: hero subtle radial glow, card hover border glow, section title gradient (yellow→purple instead of yellow→blue), progress bar gradient touch, emblem ring glow, button hover accents. Keep purple as a secondary accent — Python blue and yellow remain dominant. Purple ties back to Script House color (#a78bfa).

sprints.title: Handler Account License Code System & Database
sprints.notes: Design and implement individual handler account licensing. Problem: currently a single shared handler code — if shared it cannot be revoked per-user, creating security risk. Solution: Firestore 'handlers' collection with per-handler documents. Each handler gets a unique license code (generated by admin). Schema: { code: string (unique hash/key), assignedTo: uid|null, name: string, email: string, role: 'handler'|'senior_handler'|'admin', status: 'active'|'suspended'|'revoked', createdAt: timestamp, activatedAt: timestamp|null, lastLogin: timestamp|null, permissions: [], notes: string }. Admin panel features: generate new codes, assign to users, view all handlers, suspend/revoke individual codes instantly, audit log of handler actions. Activation flow: handler enters license code → validated against Firestore → links code to their UID → grants handler role. Code format: consider prefix like HX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX for readability. On revoke: immediately strips handler access on next auth check, no need to change other handlers' codes. Touches: AccessGuard.js (handler role check), handler-dashboard.html (activation gate), admin panel (code management), Firestore security rules, potentially Cloud Functions for code generation/validation.

Player is a security analyst drilling down through filesystem/hardware layers, inflating and popping threats. House: forge (hardware/storage excavation fits forge identity). Hold action key to inflate enemy in isolation bubble until it pops. Partially inflated enemies are stunned but recover. (3) Firewall Drop — rocks reskinned as firewall rules. Digging under a firewall block causes it to drop, crushing enemies below for bonus points. Strategic placement rewarded. ENEMY TYPES: (1) Rootkits (Pooka equivalent) — common red threats, patrol tunnels, predictable movement. Can be inflated or crushed. (2) Logic Bombs (Fygar equivalent) — green threats with ranged attack, detonate a blast radius horizontally. More dangerous, worth more points. Killing from the side (blast direction) = bonus multiplier. (3) Both enemy types go ghost-mode if left alone too long — phase through walls to hunt player (like Dig Dug's classic ghost mechanic). Ghost-mode malware has glitch/transparency visual. LEVEL PROGRESSION: Layers as difficulty tiers — (1) Userspace (2-3 enemies, slow, tutorial feel), (2) Kernel (4-5 enemies, faster, logic bombs appear), (3) Firmware (6+ enemies, mixed types, fast ghost timers), (4) Hardware (dense grid, maximum enemies, minimal safe zones). Every 3 levels a bonus round — dig for data fragments (collectibles) with no enemies, timed. SCORING: Base points for inflate-pop (scaled by depth — deeper = more points), firewall crush bonus (2x multiplier), combo for rapid kills, depth bonus per level. Collecting all data fragments in bonus round = extra life. AESTHETIC: Retro pixel-art grid, color-coded layers (blue userspace, yellow kernel, red firmware, grey hardware). Dig trail shows exposed circuitry/data paths. CRT overlay optional. Player character: small security bot with drill arm and pump attachment. IMPLEMENTATION: Tile-based grid (20x15 or similar), simple collision, sprite animation for digging/inflating/crushing. Canvas 2D, no physics engine needed. sprints.title: DNS Resolver Race — Racing Game
sprints.notes: Racing game where players compete against the clock to resolve DNS queries through the full resolution chain. CONCEPT: Player races a DNS query through the resolution hierarchy — client cache, recursive resolver, root nameserver, TLD nameserver, authoritative nameserver — choosing the correct path at each hop. Wrong hops = time penalties or dead ends. Cache hits act as speed boosts / shortcuts. GAMEPLAY IDEAS (TBD — design not finalized): (1) Side-scroller runner where the query packet is the character, lanes represent different nameserver choices, and correct hops accelerate while wrong ones slow/redirect. (2) Point-and-click path chooser: visual network map, click the correct next-hop server to advance. Timer runs throughout — faster completion = higher score. (3) Could incorporate record types (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, PTR) as different challenge modes. (4) TTL mechanic — cached records expire, forcing re-resolution through the full chain. (5) Adversary mode: DNS poisoning attacks try to redirect you to wrong servers, player must identify legitimate vs spoofed responses. EDUCATIONAL VALUE: Teaches DNS resolution process, record types, caching behavior, TTL concepts, DNS security (DNSSEC, cache poisoning). TARGET HOUSE: Web (networking fundamentals). FILE: houses/web/games/web-dns-resolver-race.html. DEPENDENCIES: None — standalone game.

sprints.title: Anti-Cheat Rule — Quiz Integrity Enforcement
sprints.notes: ANTI-CHEAT RULE: Three mandatory requirements for ALL quizzes platform-wide. (1) NO IMMEDIATE FEEDBACK — feedback, correct/incorrect indicators, and explanations must ONLY appear after the entire quiz is submitted. No green/red per question. No explanation popups mid-quiz. Review screen with explanations appears post-submission only. (2) ANSWER ROTATION — answer option positions must be randomized (Fisher-Yates shuffle) on every quiz load. Student sees A/B/C/D in different order each attempt. Correct answer index must be remapped after shuffle. (3) QUESTION POOLING — quizzes should draw from a larger question bank than displayed. Minimum: 50% more questions than shown (e.g., bank of 15, show 10). Question selection AND order randomized per attempt. AUDIT FINDINGS (228 files): 157 standalone quiz files (69%) have ALL three violations — immediate per-question feedback with green/red styling, fixed answer positions hardcoded in arrays, and identical question sets every attempt. Only 32 quizzes (~14%) use shared engines with any protections (QuizEngine.js has optional randomize/showFeedback; WSA quiz-engine.js has exam-mode with deferred feedback). 10 Cloud CSE quizzes cache full answer data in localStorage (DevTools inspectable). IMPLEMENTATION STRATEGY: Phase 1 — Update shared engines: (a) QuizEngine.js — set showFeedback:false as DEFAULT (not opt-in), ensure randomize:true is enforced not optional. Add question pool/draw mechanics. (b) WSA quiz-engine.js — already compliant on feedback deferral, add question pooling. Phase 2 — Migrate standalone quizzes: Convert the 157 standalone .quiz.html files to use QuizEngine.js with anti-cheat defaults. This is the bulk of the work. Group by house for systematic conversion: cloud (48 quizzes), forge/comptia (42 quizzes), eye/cysa (28 quizzes), shield (15 quizzes), script/linux (12 quizzes), web (8 quizzes), key (4 quizzes). Phase 3 — Question bank expansion: For each converted quiz, expand question arrays from current 10 to 15+ questions. Draw 10 per attempt. Prioritize high-traffic quizzes first (core certification tracks: A+, Security+, CySA+, Cloud+). Phase 4 — Storage cleanup: Remove localStorage caching of full answer arrays in Cloud CSE quizzes. Store only pass/fail status and score, never individual answers or correct answer keys. MARATHON SUITABILITY: Phase 1-2 are highly marathonable — systematic find-and-replace pattern across 157 files with clear before/after requirements. sprints.title: Messaging — Firestore Data Model & Security Rules
sprints.notes:
Design and implement the Firestore data model for messaging.

Collections:
- conversations/{convoId} — participants[] (2 UIDs), lastMessage (preview text), lastMessageAt (timestamp), unreadCount (map: {uid1: N, uid2: N}), createdAt
- conversations/{convoId}/messages/{msgId} — sender (UID), text (string), timestamp, read (boolean)

Security rules:
- Users can only read/write conversations where their UID is in participants[]
- Messages: sender must match auth.uid on create
- No client delete (only Cloud Functions can purge)
- Rate limit: Cloud Function validates max N messages per hour per user

Indexes:
- conversations: composite index on participants + lastMessageAt (for inbox query)
- messages: timestamp ascending (for chronological thread view)

This is the foundation — all other sub-tasks depend on it.

sprints.title: ThreatDex — Pokemon-Style Turn-Based Virus vs Antivirus Battle Game
sprints.notes:
Pokemon-inspired turn-based battle game where players collect and battle malware specimens vs security tools. Instead of catching Pokemon, you catalog threats and deploy countermeasures.

SOURCE GAME: Pokemon (Game Freak, 1996). Turn-based RPG, type effectiveness, 4 moves per creature, 6-creature party, HP/PP system, evolution, wild encounters.

CORE CONCEPT: "ThreatDex" — a digital bestiary. Player is a security analyst building their ThreatDex by encountering, analyzing, and cataloging malware in the wild. In battle, they deploy security tools against threats.

TYPE SYSTEM (replaces Pokemon's 18 types with 8 cyber types):
- MALWARE — general malicious software (strong vs Data, weak vs Sandbox)
- EXPLOIT — vulnerability attacks (strong vs Network, weak vs Patch)
- PHISHING — social engineering (strong vs Human, weak vs Training)
- NETWORK — network-layer attacks (strong vs Cloud, weak vs Firewall)
- CRYPTO — encryption/ransomware (strong vs Data, weak vs Backup)
- STEALTH — evasion/rootkits (strong vs Detection, weak vs Forensic)
- PHYSICAL — hardware attacks (strong vs Network, weak vs Policy)
- INSIDER — trusted-access threats (strong vs Policy, weak vs Monitoring)

DEFENSE TYPES (player's tools):
- FIREWALL — network defense
- SANDBOX — isolation/analysis
- PATCH — vulnerability remediation
- TRAINING — awareness/anti-phishing
- BACKUP — data recovery/anti-ransomware
- DETECTION — IDS/IPS/SIEM
- FORENSIC — investigation/analysis
- MONITORING — behavioral analysis
- POLICY — governance/compliance

Type effectiveness: 2x (super effective), 1x (normal), 0.5x (not very effective), 0x (immune). Chart creates a rock-paper-scissors web across all 8+9 types.

6 STATS per creature (mirrors Pokemon):
- HP: Hit Points (health)
- ATK: Attack power (offensive damage)
- DEF: Defense (damage reduction)
- SPD: Speed (who goes first)
- INT: Intelligence (special attack equivalent)
- RES: Resilience (special defense equivalent)

MOVES: Each creature knows 4 moves. Moves have: name, type, power, accuracy, PP (uses), effect (status/buff/debuff). Examples:
- Buffer Overflow (Exploit, 80 power, 90% acc) — may lower DEF
- Ransomware Lock (Crypto, 100 power, 85% acc) — locks 1 random move for 2 turns
- Phishing Email (Phishing, 60 power, 95% acc) — confuses target
- Port Scan (Network, 40 power, 100% acc) — always hits, reveals opponent stats
- Zero-Day Strike (Exploit, 120 power, 75% acc) — high risk/reward
- Signature Update (Detection, — power, — acc) — raises own DEF +2 stages
- Quarantine (Sandbox, 70 power, 90% acc) — traps for 1 turn
- Deep Scan (Forensic, — power, — acc) — reveals all hidden stats/moves

VIRUS ROSTER (starter 12, expandable):
1. TrojanPup → TrojanWolf → TrojanAlpha (Malware/Stealth, evolves at level 16/32)
2. PhishFry → PhishBait → PhishKing (Phishing/Network, evolves at level 14/30)
3. WormLet → WormChain → WormStorm (Network/Malware, evolves at level 15/31)
4. CryptoBit → RansomByte → RansomLord (Crypto/Exploit, evolves at level 18/36)
5. RootSeed → RootKit → RootGod (Stealth/Physical, evolves at level 20/40)
6. BotSpawn → BotNet → BotLegion (Network/Malware, evolves at level 12/28)
7. KeySniff → KeyLogger → KeyMaster (Stealth/Insider, evolves at level 16/34)
8. SQLDrop → SQLInject → SQLPwn (Exploit/Network, evolves at level 17/33)
9. ZeroBug → ZeroDay → ZeroHour (Exploit/Stealth, legendary, no evolution)
10. SpamBot → SpamFlood → SpamTsunami (Network/Phishing, evolves at level 10/25)
11. APTSeed → APTAgent → APTNation (Insider/Stealth, legendary)
12. MIMProxy → MIMAttack → MIMGod (Network/Crypto, evolves at level 19/38)

GAMEPLAY FLOW:
1. Title screen → Choose starter (pick 1 of 3: TrojanPup, PhishFry, WormLet)
2. Navigate a network map (overworld) with wild encounter zones
3. Wild encounters: random malware appears, player can Fight/Analyze(catch)/Item/Run
4. Analyze = throw a "Packet Capture" to catalog the threat (catch mechanic)
5. Gym Leaders = Security Challenges (8 bosses themed to each defense type)
6. Party of up to 6 collected threats
7. Level up via XP from battles, learn new moves at thresholds
8. Evolution at set levels (visual transformation + stat boost)

BATTLE UI:
- Split screen: player's creature bottom-left, opponent top-right
- HP bars with animated drain
- Move selection panel (4 moves + PP counts)
- Type effectiveness flash ("Super effective!" / "Not very effective...")
- Status effects: Confused, Encrypted (locked moves), Sandboxed (can't act), Scanned (stats visible)
- Switch creature mid-battle (costs a turn)

- Canvas 2D for battle scenes, DOM for menus/overworld
- Procedural pixel-art creature sprites (or simple geometric shapes with glow effects)
- State machine: overworld → encounter → battle → result → overworld
- Save/load via localStorage (party, ThreatDex, badges, position)
- Web Audio API for battle music + SFX
- Integration: GameTracker.record('threatdex', {...}), AchievementManager, GameScoreboard
- Single HTML file, shield house game
