Simulated environment with validation at each step. Both terminal commands and VS Code Docker extension workflows shown.

sprints.title: Docker Sequence — Tips, tricks & shortcuts
sprints.notes: The Docker power user module. ALIASES: alias d=docker, alias dc="docker compose", alias dps="docker ps --format table", alias dclean="docker system prune -af". SHELL TRICKS: docker exec into container with custom shell (bash || sh fallback), copy output from container to clipboard, pipe output between containers, run one-off commands (docker run --rm -it alpine sh). BUILDKIT: DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 (faster builds, better caching, secrets mounting, SSH forwarding during build), buildx for multi-platform builds. SPEED: .dockerignore reduces build context (seconds vs minutes), layer ordering for cache hits, using --target for partial multi-stage builds, parallel stage execution. COMPOSE TRICKS: docker compose up --build (rebuild on every up), docker compose run --rm service command (one-off without starting everything), extends and anchors in YAML (&anchor *alias), override files (docker-compose.override.yml auto-loaded in dev). DEBUGGING: docker run --entrypoint sh image (override entrypoint to get shell), docker history --no-trunc (see full commands in layers), docker inspect --format (Go templates for specific fields), dive tool (explore image layers interactively). VS CODE: Docker extension — right-click to run/stop/remove/logs/exec, Dockerfile IntelliSense, compose graph visualization. Before/after format: the slow way vs the trick.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Why Kubernetes & architecture overview
sprints.notes: Module 1. Start from the problem Docker alone cant solve. THE PROBLEM: you have 50 containers across 10 servers — who decides where they run? What happens when a server dies? How do you update without downtime? How do you scale? Manual docker run on each server doesnt work. WHAT K8S IS: container orchestration platform — automates deployment, scaling, and management. Not a replacement for Docker — it USES Docker (or containerd). Visual: before K8s (manual chaos) vs after K8s (orchestrated order). ARCHITECTURE: Control Plane (API Server — the front door, etcd — the database, Scheduler — where to place pods, Controller Manager — desired state loops) + Worker Nodes (kubelet — node agent, kube-proxy — networking, container runtime). Visual: full architecture diagram with arrows showing communication flow. API-driven: everything is a REST API call, kubectl is just an API client. DESIRED STATE MODEL: you declare WHAT you want (3 replicas of nginx), K8s figures out HOW to make it happen and KEEPS it that way. Reconciliation loop concept. OBJECTS: everything is a resource/object (Pod, Service, Deployment, etc.), YAML manifests describe desired state, kubectl apply sends to API server. DISTRIBUTIONS: managed K8s (EKS, AKS, GKE) vs self-hosted vs local dev (minikube, kind, k3d). For learning: minikube or kind.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — kubectl mastery (the daily driver CLI)
sprints.notes: Module 3. kubectl is to K8s what git is to version control — you use it all day every day. BASICS: kubectl get (pods, services, deployments, nodes, all), kubectl describe (detailed info + events — your first debug tool), kubectl logs (container stdout/stderr, --follow, --previous for crashed pods, --container for multi-container pods), kubectl exec -it pod -- bash (shell into pod), kubectl delete, kubectl apply -f vs kubectl create. OUTPUT FORMATTING: -o wide (extra columns), -o yaml (full YAML), -o json (for scripting), -o jsonpath (extract specific fields), -o custom-columns (build your own table), --sort-by. CONTEXT & NAMESPACE: kubectl config get-contexts (which cluster am I talking to?), kubectl config use-context, kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=prod, kubectx/kubens tools for fast switching. DRY RUN: kubectl apply --dry-run=client -o yaml (generate YAML without applying — great for learning). LABELS: kubectl get pods -l app=web, kubectl label pod mypod env=prod, kubectl get all --selector=team=backend. EXPLAIN: kubectl explain pod.spec.containers (built-in API docs — shows every field and what it means). ALIASES: alias k=kubectl, kubectl completion bash (tab completion — essential). IMPERATIVE VS DECLARATIVE: kubectl create (imperative — one-time) vs kubectl apply (declarative — idempotent, what you use in production). Quick reference card format with the 20 commands you use 80% of the time.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Services & networking (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, Ingress)
sprints.notes: Module 4. Pods get random IPs that change — Services provide stable networking. WHY SERVICES: pods are ephemeral (IP changes on restart), Service gives a stable IP + DNS name, load balances across matching pods. Visual: 3 pods behind a Service, request flows to any healthy pod. SERVICE TYPES: ClusterIP (default — internal only, other pods can reach it, used for backend APIs and databases), NodePort (exposes on every nodes IP at a static port 30000-32767, used for dev/testing), LoadBalancer (provisions cloud load balancer, used in production on EKS/AKS/GKE, gets external IP), ExternalName (DNS alias to external service). Visual: side-by-side diagrams of each type showing traffic flow from client to pod. SERVICE YAML: spec.selector (matches pod labels), spec.ports (port vs targetPort vs nodePort), spec.type. KUBE-DNS: every Service gets a DNS entry (service-name.namespace.svc.cluster.local), short names work within same namespace. INGRESS: why you dont want 50 LoadBalancers (expensive), Ingress = single entry point with path-based routing, Ingress Controller (nginx-ingress, traefik, ALB Ingress), Ingress YAML (rules, hosts, paths, TLS), visual showing domain → Ingress → multiple Services. NETWORK POLICIES: restrict pod-to-pod traffic (default = everything can talk to everything), allow/deny rules based on labels and namespaces, visual showing allowed vs blocked traffic paths. DEBUGGING: kubectl get endpoints (what IPs does the Service route to?), kubectl port-forward (access a Service from localhost without exposing), testing with curl from inside a pod.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Scaling, rolling updates & rollbacks
sprints.notes: Module 6. Scaling and zero-downtime deployments. MANUAL SCALING: kubectl scale deployment myapp --replicas=5, scaling to zero (save resources, pause service). HORIZONTAL POD AUTOSCALER (HPA): auto-scale based on CPU/memory, kubectl autoscale deployment myapp --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70, HPA YAML manifest, metrics server requirement, custom metrics (requests per second, queue depth). Visual: graph showing pod count adjusting to load over time. ROLLING UPDATES: the default strategy — Deployment updates pods gradually (new version pods come up while old ones terminate), strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge (how many extra pods during update), maxUnavailable (how many can be down), visual: step-by-step diagram showing old pods replaced by new pods with zero downtime. kubectl rollout status (watch the update), kubectl rollout history (see revision history). ROLLBACK: kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp (instant rollback to previous version), kubectl rollout undo --to-revision=3 (specific version), why rollback is fast (ReplicaSet for previous version still exists, just scales it back up). RECREATE STRATEGY: kill all old → start all new (has downtime, use for stateful apps that cant run two versions). CANARY DEPLOYMENTS: concept — route small % of traffic to new version, monitor, then full rollout. Blue/green deployments via Service selector swapping. Visual: canary showing 90% traffic to v1, 10% to v2.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Storage (PV, PVC, StorageClasses)
sprints.notes: Module 7. Persistent data in an ephemeral world. THE PROBLEM: pod dies → local data gone (same as Docker). K8s needs a way to decouple storage from pod lifecycle. VOLUMES: emptyDir (shared between containers in same pod, dies with pod), hostPath (mount host directory — avoid in production), projected volumes (combine configmaps/secrets/downwardAPI). PERSISTENT VOLUMES (PV): cluster-level storage resource, provisioned by admin, exists independently of pods. Visual: PV as a disk icon living outside any pod. PERSISTENT VOLUME CLAIMS (PVC): pod requests storage via PVC, K8s binds PVC to matching PV (like a storage voucher). Visual: Pod → PVC → PV → actual disk. Access modes: ReadWriteOnce (single node), ReadOnlyMany (multiple nodes read), ReadWriteMany (multiple nodes read-write — NFS/EFS). STORAGE CLASSES: dynamic provisioning — no admin needed, PVC requests a StorageClass and PV is auto-created, cloud providers (gp3 on AWS, pd-ssd on GCP, managed-premium on Azure). Reclaim policies: Retain (keep data), Delete (destroy with PVC). STATEFULSETS: when you need stable network identity + persistent storage per pod (databases, message queues), pod names are ordinal (mysql-0, mysql-1, mysql-2), volumeClaimTemplates. Visual: StatefulSet vs Deployment comparison diagram.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Namespaces, RBAC & multi-tenancy
sprints.notes: Module 8. Organizing and securing a shared cluster. NAMESPACES: virtual clusters within a cluster, default namespaces (default, kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease), creating namespaces, when to use (per team, per environment, per project), resource isolation. kubectl get pods -n production, kubectl get pods --all-namespaces. RESOURCE QUOTAS: limit CPU/memory/pod count per namespace, prevent one team from consuming entire cluster. LimitRange: default requests/limits for pods in namespace. RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): who can do what where. Subjects (Users, Groups, ServiceAccounts), Resources (pods, services, secrets), Verbs (get, list, create, delete, watch). Role + RoleBinding (namespace-scoped), ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-wide). YAML walkthrough for each. Visual: RBAC chain — User → RoleBinding → Role → allowed actions on resources. SERVICE ACCOUNTS: identity for pods (not humans), default ServiceAccount per namespace, pod uses ServiceAccount to authenticate to API server, least-privilege principle. SECURITY CONTEXTS: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, seccompProfile, pod-level vs container-level. Practical: set up namespace with quotas and RBAC so dev team can only access their own namespace.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Helm (package manager for Kubernetes)
sprints.notes: Module 9. Writing raw YAML for every app doesnt scale. WHY HELM: managing dozens of YAML files per app is painful, environment differences (dev vs prod) mean duplicated manifests, Helm solves this with templating and packaging. CONCEPTS: Charts (package of K8s manifests + templates), Releases (installed instance of a chart), Repositories (chart storage — like Docker Hub for Helm). CHART ANATOMY: Chart.yaml (metadata), values.yaml (defaults — the knobs users turn), templates/ directory (Go-templated K8s manifests), helpers.tpl (reusable template functions). Visual: values.yaml + template → rendered manifest. COMMANDS: helm repo add/update, helm search repo, helm install myrelease chart (deploy), helm upgrade (update), helm rollback (undo), helm uninstall (remove), helm list (see releases), helm status, helm history. VALUES: helm install -f myvalues.yaml (override defaults), --set key=value (inline override), values hierarchy (chart defaults → -f overrides → --set overrides). CREATING CHARTS: helm create mychart (scaffold), writing templates ({{ .Values.image.repository }}), conditionals ({{ if }}), loops ({{ range }}), named templates ({{ include }}). POPULAR CHARTS: nginx-ingress, cert-manager, prometheus, grafana — dont reinvent the wheel. HELMFILE: managing multiple charts across environments. Best practice: use Helm for third-party tools, consider Kustomize for your own apps.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Monitoring, logging & debugging
sprints.notes: Module 10. Things break — you need to find out why fast. DEBUGGING WORKFLOW: kubectl describe pod (check Events section first — scheduling failures, image pull errors, OOM kills), kubectl logs (application output, --previous for crashed pods), kubectl exec (shell in for live debugging), kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp. COMMON ISSUES AND FIXES: ImagePullBackOff (wrong image name, private registry auth), CrashLoopBackOff (app crashing — check logs, check command/args, check env vars), Pending (no node has enough resources, check kubectl describe node), OOMKilled (container exceeded memory limit — increase or fix leak), CreateContainerConfigError (missing ConfigMap or Secret). Visual: decision tree — pod not running? follow this flowchart. RESOURCE MONITORING: kubectl top pods/nodes (requires metrics-server), resource requests vs limits (requests = guaranteed minimum, limits = hard ceiling), QoS classes (Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort). OBSERVABILITY STACK: Prometheus (metrics collection, PromQL basics), Grafana (dashboards, pre-built K8s dashboards), Loki (log aggregation), alerting concepts. HEALTH PROBES: livenessProbe (is the container alive? restart if not), readinessProbe (is it ready for traffic? remove from Service if not), startupProbe (slow-starting containers). Probe types: httpGet, exec, tcpSocket, grpc. Visual: probe decision diagram — when each probe runs and what happens on failure.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Real-world patterns & production readiness
sprints.notes: Module 11. Production K8s patterns that real teams use. POD DESIGN PATTERNS: sidecar (logging/proxy containers alongside main app — Envoy, Fluentd), init containers (run setup tasks before app starts — migrations, config fetching, wait-for-db), ambassador (proxy to external service). RESOURCE MANAGEMENT: always set requests AND limits, right-sizing (start conservative, adjust based on metrics), Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) for automatic right-sizing. POD DISRUPTION BUDGETS: PDB ensures minimum availability during voluntary disruptions (node upgrades, scaling down), minAvailable or maxUnavailable. AFFINITY & ANTI-AFFINITY: control pod placement — spread across availability zones (podAntiAffinity), co-locate related pods (podAffinity), node affinity (run on GPU nodes). TAINTS & TOLERATIONS: reserve nodes for specific workloads, NoSchedule/PreferNoSchedule/NoExecute. JOBS & CRONJOBS: batch processing (Job runs to completion, parallelism, backoff limit), scheduled tasks (CronJob — K8s equivalent of cron, schedule syntax, concurrencyPolicy, successfulJobsHistoryLimit). KUSTOMIZE: template-free customization — base + overlays for environments, strategic merge patches, commonLabels/commonAnnotations. GITOPS: ArgoCD/Flux concepts — Git as single source of truth, auto-sync cluster state to repo, visual showing git push → ArgoCD detects → applies to cluster. PRODUCTION CHECKLIST: resource limits set, health probes configured, PDB defined, security context locked down, namespaces and RBAC configured, monitoring and alerting active, backup strategy for stateful workloads.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Hands-on lab (deploy, scale, update, debug)
sprints.notes: Comprehensive hands-on lab in simulated K8s environment. Challenge sequence: (1) Create namespace and set context, (2) Write Deployment YAML from scratch (3 replicas, resource limits, health probes), (3) Create Service to expose the app (ClusterIP), (4) Create Ingress for external access, (5) Create ConfigMap and mount into pods, (6) Scale up to 5 replicas manually, (7) Set up HPA for auto-scaling, (8) Perform rolling update to new image version, (9) Rollback when new version has a bug, (10) Debug a CrashLoopBackOff pod (check describe, logs, exec), (11) Install a Helm chart (nginx-ingress), (12) Clean up namespace. Visual commit-graph-style progress showing each challenge completed. Both kubectl commands and VS Code K8s extension shown.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Tips, tricks & shortcuts
sprints.notes: The K8s power user module. ALIASES: alias k=kubectl, alias kgp="kubectl get pods", alias kgs="kubectl get svc", alias kgd="kubectl get deploy", alias kd="kubectl describe", alias kl="kubectl logs", alias ke="kubectl exec -it". SPEED: kubectl completion bash >> ~/.bashrc (tab completion changes everything), kubectx + kubens (switch context/namespace in one command), kubectl get all (see everything in namespace), kube-ps1 (show current context/namespace in shell prompt). GENERATORS: kubectl run nginx --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > pod.yaml (generate YAML from command line), kubectl create deployment --dry-run=client -o yaml, kubectl expose --dry-run=client -o yaml — never write YAML from scratch again. DEBUGGING: kubectl run debug --rm -it --image=busybox -- sh (temporary debug pod), kubectl port-forward svc/myservice 8080:80 (access without exposing), kubectl cp pod:/path/file ./local (extract files), kubectl auth can-i create pods (check your permissions), kubectl get events --field-selector reason=Failed. JSONPATH: kubectl get pods -o jsonpath="{.items[*].metadata.name}" (extract data for scripting), kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath="{.items[*].status.addresses[0].address}" (get all node IPs). VS CODE: Kubernetes extension — cluster explorer, apply manifests, stream logs, port forward, Helm chart support. K9S: terminal UI for K8s (like htop for your cluster) — navigate pods/services/deployments with keyboard, real-time logs, exec, delete. EXAM PREP: these shortcuts are critical for CKA/CKAD timed exams.

sprints.title: Data Formats & Serialization — YAML, JSON, TOML
sprints.notes: Foundation module — prerequisite for Docker Compose, K8s manifests, CI/CD pipelines, package configs. Covers: YAML (indentation, anchors, multi-doc), JSON (syntax, nesting, schema), TOML (tables, arrays, inline), format comparison matrix. Hands-on: convert between formats, validate syntax, common gotchas (YAML indentation, JSON trailing commas, quoting rules). Visual: side-by-side format comparisons showing the same config in YAML vs JSON vs TOML.

sprints.title: Config File Formats — XML, INI, ENV, HCL
sprints.notes: Covers legacy and specialized formats: XML (elements, attributes, namespaces — Maven pom.xml, .NET configs), INI/conf (sections, key-value — .gitconfig, systemd units, nginx.conf), ENV (.env files, dotenv, shell export, secrets management tie-in to DO-33), HCL (Terraform syntax preview, ties into DO-23/24). When to use which format, real-world examples from each tool ecosystem.

sprints.title: CI/CD Fundamentals — Why Automate Everything
sprints.notes: Conceptual foundation before any tooling. Covers: what is Continuous Integration (merge early, merge often, automated testing), what is Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment (the difference matters), the pipeline mental model (source → build → test → stage → deploy), benefits (fast feedback, reduced risk, repeatable releases), anti-patterns (manual gates everywhere, deploy Fridays, works on my machine). History: from waterfall to agile to DevOps to GitOps. Visual: pipeline flow diagram, CI vs CD vs CD comparison chart, the deployment confidence curve. Real-world horror stories: what happens without CI/CD.

sprints.title: Pipeline Architecture — Stages, Jobs & Dependencies
sprints.notes: How pipelines are structured regardless of platform. Covers: stages (build, test, deploy), jobs within stages, steps within jobs, parallel vs sequential execution, job dependencies (needs/requires), conditional execution (if/when/rules), fan-out/fan-in patterns, pipeline-as-code philosophy, DAG (directed acyclic graph) execution model. Artifact passing between jobs, workspace persistence, caching strategies. Visual: DAG diagrams showing job graphs, stage gates, parallel branches merging. Compare: how the same pipeline looks in GitHub Actions vs GitLab CI vs Jenkins.

sprints.title: Testing in Pipelines — Quality Gates & Coverage
sprints.notes: The CI in CI/CD — automated testing is the whole point. Covers: test pyramid (unit → integration → E2E), when to run which tests (PR vs merge vs nightly), test runners in CI (Jest, pytest, Go test), code coverage collection & reporting (Codecov, Coveralls), coverage thresholds as quality gates, test result reporting (JUnit XML, annotations on PRs), flaky test detection & quarantine, parallel test execution (sharding, splitting), security scanning (SAST, dependency audit, license check), linting as a pipeline stage. Visual: test pyramid diagram, PR check annotations screenshot. Hands-on: add test + coverage + lint stages to a pipeline.

sprints.title: Build & Artifact Management
sprints.notes: What happens between test and deploy. Covers: build steps (compile, bundle, transpile, minify), build artifacts (binaries, Docker images, static sites, packages), artifact storage (GitHub Packages, npm registry, Docker Hub, S3, Artifactory), versioning strategies (semver, CalVer, git SHA), automated versioning (semantic-release, conventional commits), build reproducibility (lock files, pinned dependencies, deterministic builds), build caching (layer caching for Docker, node_modules caching, build output caching), multi-platform builds (cross-compilation, Docker buildx). Visual: artifact lifecycle diagram from source to registry to deployment.

sprints.title: Deployment Strategies — Zero-Downtime Releases
sprints.notes: How code gets to production safely. Covers: deployment strategies comparison — rolling update (gradual replacement), blue/green (parallel environments, instant switch), canary (percentage-based rollout, metrics-driven promotion), A/B testing (feature-flag driven), recreate (stop old, start new — when it's OK). Rollback strategies: automatic rollback on health check failure, manual rollback procedures, database rollback considerations. Feature flags (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, custom), dark launches, traffic shifting. Environment promotion: dev → staging → production, environment parity, configuration drift. Visual: animated diagrams showing each strategy's traffic flow. Real-world: when Netflix, GitHub, Google use each strategy.

sprints.title: Secrets & Environment Management in CI/CD
sprints.notes: Security in pipelines — the most common thing done wrong. Covers: GitHub Actions secrets (repo, environment, org-level), secret masking in logs, OIDC for cloud authentication (no stored credentials), environment-specific variables, .env files vs CI secrets vs vault, secret rotation strategies, least-privilege service accounts, GitHub Environments (protection rules, required reviewers, wait timers, deployment branches). External secrets: HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault integration. Anti-patterns: hardcoded secrets, secrets in Docker images, printing secrets to logs. Hands-on: configure OIDC auth for cloud deployment, set up environment protection rules.

sprints.title: CI/CD Platforms — GitLab CI, Jenkins & Beyond
sprints.notes: GitHub Actions isn't the only game in town. Covers: GitLab CI (.gitlab-ci.yml syntax, stages, jobs, runners, Auto DevOps, built-in container registry), Jenkins (Jenkinsfile declarative vs scripted, plugins ecosystem, Blue Ocean, distributed builds, shared libraries), CircleCI (orbs, config.yml, Docker executor, workflows), Azure DevOps Pipelines (YAML pipelines, classic editor, self-hosted agents, Azure integration), AWS CodePipeline/CodeBuild, Google Cloud Build. Comparison matrix: features, pricing, hosting options, ecosystem, learning curve. When to choose what: startup vs enterprise, cloud-native vs hybrid, open-source vs managed. Hands-on: translate a GitHub Actions workflow to GitLab CI.

sprints.title: Pipeline Monitoring, Notifications & Observability
sprints.notes: Pipelines are only useful if you know when they break. Covers: build notifications (Slack, Teams, email, webhook), status badges in README, pipeline dashboards & metrics (build duration trends, failure rates, MTTR, deployment frequency — the DORA metrics), log aggregation from CI runs, structured logging in pipelines, alerting on pipeline failures, monitoring post-deployment (health checks, smoke tests, synthetic monitoring), observability-driven deployment (metrics-based canary promotion/rollback). GitHub: commit status checks, deployment status API, check runs. Visual: DORA metrics dashboard, pipeline health over time charts.

sprints.title: CI/CD Tips, Tricks & Battle Scars
sprints.notes: Hard-won wisdom from production pipelines. Covers: speed optimization (caching everything, parallel jobs, skip CI for docs, path filtering, timeout tuning), cost management (self-hosted runners, spot instances, concurrency limits), debugging failed pipelines (act for local GitHub Actions testing, SSH into runners, step-level debugging), pipeline security (supply chain attacks, action pinning by SHA not tag, Dependabot for actions, least-privilege tokens, CODEOWNERS for workflow files), monorepo strategies (path-based triggers, affected-project detection), GitOps workflow (ArgoCD, Flux — declarative deployments from Git). Anti-patterns hall of shame: 45-minute pipelines, deploy-on-Friday bots, YOLO to production.

sprints.title: Infrastructure as Code — Why Code Your Cloud
sprints.notes: Conceptual foundation before any IaC tooling. Covers: what is Infrastructure as Code (infra defined in text files, version-controlled, repeatable), imperative vs declarative approaches (scripts vs desired state), idempotency (run it 10 times, same result), immutable vs mutable infrastructure (pets vs cattle), infrastructure drift (what it is, why it’s dangerous, how to detect it), the IaC workflow (write → plan → review → apply → verify). Benefits: consistency, speed, documentation-as-code, disaster recovery, auditability, collaboration. History: from manual provisioning to CloudFormation to Terraform to Pulumi. Visual: manual vs IaC comparison, pets vs cattle diagram, drift detection flowchart. Real-world: what happens when you manage 500 servers by hand.

sprints.title: Terraform State — The Source of Truth
sprints.notes: The most critical and most misunderstood part of Terraform. Covers: what is state (mapping between config and real-world resources), terraform.tfstate file anatomy (JSON structure, resource addresses, metadata), local vs remote state (why local state breaks teams), remote backends (S3 + DynamoDB, Terraform Cloud, Azure Blob, GCS), state locking (why it exists, what happens without it, lock timeouts), state commands (terraform state list, show, mv, rm, pull, push), importing existing resources (terraform import, import blocks in 1.5+), moved blocks (refactoring without destroy/recreate), state file security (sensitive data in state, encryption at rest, access controls), workspace isolation (terraform workspace for environment separation). Visual: state file anatomy diagram, remote backend architecture. Anti-patterns: committing state to git, shared local state, manual state editing.

sprints.title: Terraform Modules — Reusable Infrastructure
sprints.notes: Writing DRY, maintainable Terraform at scale. Covers: what are modules (encapsulated, reusable infrastructure packages), module structure (main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf, versions.tf), root module vs child modules, local modules (./modules/vpc), remote modules (Terraform Registry, Git repos, S3), module versioning & version constraints, input variables & validation, output values & cross-module references, module composition (calling modules from modules), Terraform Registry (official vs community, publishing your own). Design patterns: module per component, module per environment, module per service. Anti-patterns: mega-modules, hardcoded values, tight coupling. Visual: module dependency tree, module interface diagram. Hands-on: refactor a flat config into reusable modules.

sprints.title: Ansible Fundamentals — Agentless Automation
sprints.notes: Track opener — why Ansible dominates. Covers: Ansible architecture (control node, managed nodes, no agent required, SSH/WinRM transport, push model vs pull model), installation (pip, package manager, version management), first commands (ansible --version, ansible all -m ping, ad-hoc commands), configuration (ansible.cfg precedence — env var, project, home, /etc), connection types (SSH, WinRM, local, Docker, network_cli), Python requirements on managed nodes, ansible vs ansible-playbook vs ansible-galaxy vs ansible-vault vs ansible-console CLI tools. Visual: architecture diagram showing control node → SSH → managed nodes, comparison with agent-based tools. Hands-on: install Ansible, configure a project, run ad-hoc commands against local and remote hosts.

sprints.title: Automation Landscape — Ansible, Chef, Puppet & Salt
sprints.notes: The big picture before diving into any track. Covers: what is configuration management (desired state, convergence, idempotency), the four major tools comparison — Ansible (agentless, YAML, push, Red Hat), Chef (agent, Ruby DSL, pull, Progress), Puppet (agent, Puppet DSL, pull, Perforce), Salt (agent optional, YAML/Python, push+pull, VMware). Comparison matrix: architecture, language, learning curve, community, enterprise offering, certification paths, job market demand. Imperative vs declarative approaches, push vs pull models, agentless vs agent-based tradeoffs. When to choose what: team size, existing skills, infrastructure scale, cloud-native vs on-prem. Brief intro to newer tools: Terraform for provisioning (not config mgmt — know the difference), Pulumi, CDK. Visual: comparison matrix, architecture diagrams for each tool, market share/trends chart. This module sets up the Ansible track (primary) with future tracks for Chef, Puppet, Salt.

sprints.title: IaC Platforms — CloudFormation, Pulumi & CDK
sprints.notes: Terraform isn’t the only option — know the landscape. Covers: AWS CloudFormation (JSON/YAML templates, stacks, change sets, drift detection, StackSets for multi-account, deep AWS integration), AWS CDK (infrastructure in TypeScript/Python/Java, constructs, synth to CloudFormation), Pulumi (infrastructure in real programming languages — TypeScript, Python, Go, C# — state management, Pulumi Cloud, vs Terraform), Azure Bicep (ARM template evolution, declarative Azure-native), Google Cloud Deployment Manager. Comparison matrix: language, cloud support, state management, community, learning curve, enterprise features. When to choose what: multi-cloud vs single-cloud, team skills, existing ecosystem. Hands-on: deploy the same resource in Terraform vs CloudFormation vs Pulumi — see the differences.

sprints.title: IaC Testing & Policy — Validate Before You Apply
sprints.notes: Catching infrastructure bugs before they hit production. Covers: static analysis (terraform validate, terraform fmt, tflint — custom rules, provider-specific checks), security scanning (checkov, tfsec, Snyk IaC — CIS benchmarks, compliance), policy-as-code (Open Policy Agent/Rego, Sentinel for Terraform Cloud, AWS Service Control Policies), cost estimation (Infracost — PR comments with cost impact), plan review (terraform plan output analysis, automated plan in CI), testing frameworks (Terratest in Go — integration testing, kitchen-terraform, terraform-compliance BDD), Ansible testing (ansible-lint, molecule for role testing, yamllint), pre-commit hooks for IaC (format, validate, scan on every commit). Visual: IaC validation pipeline diagram showing lint → validate → scan → plan → cost → apply. Hands-on: set up a pre-commit + CI validation pipeline for Terraform.

sprints.title: GitOps for Infrastructure — PRs That Build Clouds
sprints.notes: The convergence of Git workflow and infrastructure management. Covers: GitOps principles (Git as single source of truth, declarative desired state, automated reconciliation, continuous observation), GitOps for infrastructure (infra changes via PRs, automated terraform plan on PR, apply on merge, drift reconciliation), Atlantis (self-hosted Terraform automation — plan/apply from PR comments, locking, policy checks), Terraform Cloud/Enterprise (remote runs, VCS integration, private registry, Sentinel policies, cost estimation), Spacelift, env0, Scalr — managed Terraform platforms. ArgoCD & Flux for Kubernetes GitOps (declarative K8s deployments from Git, sync policies, health checks). Anti-patterns: ClickOps alongside GitOps, manual applies, shared workspaces without locking. Visual: GitOps loop diagram, PR-driven infrastructure workflow.

sprints.title: IaC Tips, Tricks & War Stories
sprints.notes: Hard-won wisdom from managing real infrastructure as code. Covers: Terraform tricks (terragrunt for DRY configs, workspaces vs directory structure for environments, terraform console for debugging, -target for surgical applies, moved blocks for painless refactoring, lifecycle rules for zero-downtime), Ansible tricks (ansible-pull for decentralized, callback plugins, custom modules, strategy plugins — free vs linear), blast radius management (small state files, account-per-environment, progressive rollouts), disaster recovery (state backup, state recovery procedures, terraform force-unlock), migration strategies (importing brownfield infra, gradual adoption, strangler fig pattern for IaC), collaboration patterns (module ownership, PR review checklists for IaC, documentation-as-code with terraform-docs). Anti-patterns hall of shame: 10,000-line main.tf, state file in Dropbox, terraform apply -auto-approve in production.

sprints.title: Ansible Inventory — Know Your Fleet
sprints.notes: Ansible track module 2 — you can't automate what you can't target. Covers: static inventory (INI format, YAML format, multiple inventory files), groups (defining, nesting, group_of_groups), host patterns (all, ungrouped, wildcards, regex, intersection &, exclusion !), host_vars and group_vars (directory structure, variable files, precedence), default groups (all, ungrouped), inventory parameters (ansible_host, ansible_port, ansible_user, ansible_ssh_private_key_file, ansible_python_interpreter), dynamic inventory (scripts, plugins — aws_ec2, azure_rm, gcp_compute, docker, kubernetes), inventory plugins (auto, constructed, generator), caching inventory, multiple inventory sources, inventory graph (ansible-inventory --graph). Visual: inventory hierarchy diagram, group inheritance visualization. Hands-on: build a multi-group inventory, use host/group vars, set up dynamic inventory from a cloud provider.

sprints.title: Ansible Playbooks — Automating Everything
sprints.notes: Ansible track module 3 — the core of Ansible automation. Covers: playbook anatomy (YAML, plays, hosts, tasks, become), task structure (name, module, args, register, when, loop, notify, tags, block/rescue/always), play-level directives (hosts, become, vars, vars_files, gather_facts, strategy, serial, max_fail_percentage), execution order (pre_tasks, roles, tasks, post_tasks, handlers), conditionals (when — comparisons, logical operators, defined/undefined, failed/changed/skipped), loops (loop, with_items, with_dict, with_fileglob, loop_control — index_var, label, pause), blocks (grouping tasks, error handling with rescue/always — Ansible's try/catch), includes vs imports (static vs dynamic — include_tasks, import_tasks, include_role, import_role), check mode (--check, --diff, check_mode per task). Visual: playbook execution flow diagram, task state machine. Hands-on: write playbooks for common scenarios — user management, package installation, service configuration, multi-play orchestration.

sprints.title: Ansible Modules & Collections — The Toolbox
sprints.notes: Ansible track module 4 — 3000+ modules organized into collections. Covers: what are modules (units of work, idempotent, return JSON), essential modules deep dive — command/shell/raw (when to use which, avoid when possible), copy/template/file (file management), package/apt/yum/dnf (package management), service/systemd (service management), user/group (user management), lineinfile/blockinfile/replace (file editing), uri/get_url (HTTP operations), git (repo management), debug/assert/fail (debugging & validation). Collections (ansible.builtin, community.general, cloud collections), Ansible Galaxy (installing collections, requirements.yml, collection versioning), finding the right module (ansible-doc, online docs), module return values (changed, failed, msg, stdout, rc), registering results and using them in conditionals. Visual: module category map, collection namespace hierarchy. Hands-on: solve real tasks using the right module — not just command/shell for everything.

sprints.title: Ansible Roles — Reusable Automation Packages
sprints.notes: Ansible track module 5 — the role is Ansible's unit of reuse. Covers: role directory structure (tasks/, handlers/, templates/, files/, vars/, defaults/, meta/, tests/), role creation (ansible-galaxy role init), defaults vs vars (defaults are overridable, vars are not — precedence matters), role dependencies (meta/main.yml — dependencies list, allow_duplicates), role execution order (dependencies first, then role tasks), Ansible Galaxy (browsing, installing, requirements.yml, versioning, private Galaxy servers), writing quality roles (parametrize everything, sensible defaults, platform support with when + ansible_os_family), role testing with Molecule (init, drivers — Docker/Vagrant/cloud, converge, verify, test matrix), role documentation (README.md, meta/main.yml metadata, argument_specs). Visual: role directory tree, role dependency resolution diagram. Hands-on: build a reusable role for a web server, publish to Galaxy, test with Molecule.

sprints.title: Ansible Variables & Facts — Data-Driven Automation
sprints.notes: Ansible track module 6 — the 46 levels of variable precedence. Covers: variable sources (inventory, playbook, role defaults, role vars, task vars, extra vars, facts, magic vars, registered vars), the full precedence order (from lowest to highest — role defaults → inventory → playbook → role vars → task vars → extra vars), gathering facts (setup module, ansible_facts, custom facts in /etc/ansible/facts.d/), fact caching (JSON, Redis, memcached), magic variables (inventory_hostname, groups, hostvars, ansible_play_hosts, ansible_check_mode, role_path), special variables (omit, undefined), variable scoping (global, play, host, task), set_fact vs register (when to use which), prompting for input (vars_prompt), encrypting variables (vault inline, vault files — preview for DO-93). Visual: variable precedence pyramid, fact gathering flow. Hands-on: debug variable resolution, use facts for conditional platform logic, set up fact caching.

sprints.title: Ansible Templates & Jinja2 — Dynamic Configuration
sprints.notes: Ansible track module 7 — turning static configs into dynamic templates. Covers: Jinja2 basics (variables {{ }}, statements {% %}, comments {# #}), filters (default, join, select, reject, map, regex_replace, to_yaml, to_json, b64encode, hash, ternary, combine), tests (defined, undefined, string, number, iterable, mapping, match, search), conditionals in templates ({% if %}/{% elif %}/{% else %}/{% endif %}), loops in templates ({% for %}/{% endfor %}, loop.index, loop.first, loop.last), whitespace control (-, +, trim_blocks, lstrip_blocks), template inheritance ({% extends %}/{% block %}), macros ({% macro %} — reusable template functions), the template module (src, dest, owner, group, mode, validate, backup), template best practices (validate config before deploying, backup originals, comment with 'Managed by Ansible'). Visual: template rendering pipeline diagram, before/after config file comparison. Hands-on: template nginx.conf, Apache vhosts, systemd units, application configs with environment-specific values.

sprints.title: Ansible Vault — Secrets Management
sprints.notes: Ansible track module 8 — keeping secrets out of Git. Covers: ansible-vault commands (create, encrypt, decrypt, edit, view, rekey, encrypt_string), vault passwords (prompt, password file, script, multiple vault IDs), encrypting entire files vs inline variables (encrypt_string for single values in otherwise plain YAML), vault ID labels (dev, staging, prod — different passwords per environment), vault in playbooks (--ask-vault-pass, --vault-password-file, --vault-id), vault best practices (encrypt only what's sensitive, use vault IDs, rotate passwords, never commit unencrypted secrets), integration with external secret managers (HashiCorp Vault lookup plugin, AWS SSM, Azure Key Vault), ansible-vault in CI/CD (vault password from CI secrets, avoid password files in repos). Visual: encryption/decryption flow diagram, vault ID resolution. Hands-on: encrypt database credentials, use vault IDs for multi-environment secrets, integrate with an external secret manager.

sprints.title: Ansible AWX & Automation Platform — Enterprise Scale
sprints.notes: Ansible track module 9 — from CLI to enterprise platform. Covers: AWX (open-source upstream of Automation Platform, web UI for Ansible), installation (Docker Compose, Kubernetes operator, Minikube for lab), core concepts — Organizations, Teams, Users, RBAC (role-based access control), Projects (Git-backed playbook sources, SCM sync), Inventories (static, dynamic sources, smart inventories), Credentials (machine, SCM, vault, cloud — secure credential storage), Job Templates (playbook + inventory + credentials + survey = one-click automation), Surveys (runtime prompts — variable input forms for non-technical users), Workflows (chaining job templates, conditional paths, approval nodes), Schedules (cron-like recurring jobs), Notifications (Slack, email, webhook on job success/failure), API (RESTful, everything automatable — jobs, inventories, credentials via API). Visual: AWX dashboard screenshots, workflow designer diagram. Hands-on: deploy AWX locally, create a project, build a job template with survey, chain workflows.

sprints.title: Ansible for Cloud & Networking
sprints.notes: Ansible track module 10 — Ansible automates more than just Linux servers. Covers: cloud provisioning (amazon.aws collection — ec2_instance, s3_bucket, vpc, security_group, rds; azure.azcollection; google.cloud), dynamic inventory from cloud (aws_ec2 plugin, azure_rm plugin — auto-discover running instances), cloud modules vs Terraform (when to use Ansible for cloud, when to use Terraform, when to use both), network automation (cisco.ios, arista.eos, juniper.junos, vyos — network_cli connection), network modules (ios_config, ios_command, cli_config, net_get/net_put), network inventory patterns (platform-specific groups, network_os variable), Windows automation (win_* modules, WinRM connection, win_chocolatey, win_service, win_feature, win_dsc), container automation (community.docker, kubernetes.core — manage containers and K8s resources). Visual: multi-platform automation diagram showing Ansible reaching cloud, network, Windows, containers. Hands-on: provision cloud resources, configure network devices, manage Windows hosts — all from one Ansible control node.

sprints.title: Ansible Testing & CI Integration
sprints.notes: Ansible track module 11 — trust but verify. Covers: linting (ansible-lint — rules, profiles, custom rules, .ansible-lint config, yamllint integration), Molecule (test framework for roles — init, create, converge, idempotence, verify, destroy, drivers: Docker/Podman/Vagrant/cloud, verifiers: Ansible/testinfra/goss, test matrix for multiple platforms), check mode & diff mode (--check --diff, simulating changes, check_mode per task), assert module (validating state in playbooks), CI/CD integration (GitHub Actions + Molecule, GitLab CI + ansible-lint, Jenkins pipeline for Ansible), testing strategies (unit: molecule converge + verify, integration: full stack deploy + test, smoke: post-deployment health checks), playbook debugging (ansible-playbook -vvvv, debug module, debugger keyword, callback plugins — yaml, json, timer), performance testing (profiling with callback plugins, identifying slow tasks). Visual: Molecule test lifecycle diagram, CI pipeline for Ansible roles. Hands-on: add Molecule tests to a role, set up CI pipeline, debug a failing playbook.

sprints.title: Ansible Real-World Patterns & Lab
sprints.notes: Ansible track module 12 — putting it all together. Covers: real-world automation patterns — rolling updates (serial, max_fail_percentage, delegate_to for load balancer drain), blue/green deployments with Ansible, zero-downtime deployment playbooks, multi-tier application deployment (web + app + db, play-per-tier, delegation, run_once), compliance scanning (ansible-lint + custom rules, CIS benchmark playbooks), patch management (yum/apt update, reboot handling with wait_for_connection, maintenance windows), backup automation, monitoring agent deployment, user onboarding/offboarding. Project structure at scale (directory layout, environment separation, ansible.cfg per project, requirements.yml for dependencies). Anti-patterns: shell/command for everything, 1000-line playbooks, no error handling, running as root unnecessarily. Lab: deploy a full multi-tier application stack — provisioning, configuration, deployment, verification, rollback.

sprints.title: Ansible Tips, Tricks & Dark Arts
sprints.notes: Ansible track module 13 — hard-won wisdom. Covers: performance tuning (pipelining, ControlPersist, mitogen, forks, async + poll for long tasks, free strategy for independent hosts), callback plugins (yaml output, timer, profile_tasks — find slow tasks), custom modules (Python, write your own when built-ins don't fit), custom filters & plugins (filter_plugins/, lookup_plugins/, connection_plugins/), Ansible Navigator (next-gen CLI, TUI, EE integration), Execution Environments (containerized Ansible, ansible-builder, reproducible automation), ansible-pull (decentralized — nodes pull their own config from Git), event-driven Ansible (ansible-rulebook, Event-Driven Automation controller, webhook triggers), Ansible + Terraform integration patterns (Terraform provisions, Ansible configures, dynamic inventory bridge), migration tips (from shell scripts to Ansible, from Chef/Puppet to Ansible). Secret tricks: delegate_to localhost for API calls, throttle for rate-limited APIs, meta: clear_facts/clear_host_errors/end_play/end_host, ansible-inventory --graph --vars for debugging.

sprints.title: Admin Progress Reset — Handler tool to clear/reset student module completion
sprints.description: Add a handler-facing tool (in handler dashboard or admin panel) that lets instructors reset a specific module completion for a specific student. Use cases: module got stuck/locked, content was updated and needs re-completion, student progress is corrupt. Should support: (1) reset single module for one student, (2) reset entire district for one student, (3) bulk reset a module across all students (e.g. after content fix). Needs Firestore writes with handler-level auth check. Consider adding audit log so resets are traceable.

sprints.title: In-App Issue Reporter — Auto-submit bug/feedback to Firestore
sprints.description: Replace the broken GitHub Issues link in dashboard footer with an in-app issue reporter. Small modal form: type dropdown (bug/feedback/question) + text field. Auto-captures context: current URL, user UID, browser info, timestamp, module ID if on a module page. Writes to Firestore issues/{docId} collection. Handler dashboard gets a new Issues section to view/triage/resolve submissions. No external dependencies, student never leaves the app.

sprints.title: Linux Admin Hub — Add Completion Stamps to All Modules
sprints.notes: Add visual completion stamps to every module in the Linux Administration district hub. When a user has completed a presentation/lab/quiz, the module card should show a stamp or badge indicating completion. Scoped to the LA hub only (linux-admin district, 36 modules). Related to F-39 (Universal Completion Stamps) but this is the focused first pass for one district. MARATHON SUITABILITY: Repetitive per-module work, autonomous, no design decisions needed once pattern is established.
